FINDING 1 -- THE RULE IS KEYED ON THE COLON, AND A DECLARED EXCLUSION DOES NOT NEED ONE. Driven, all four counted as COVERAGE by the shipped regex: a set literal EXCLUDE = {'w.py', 'x.py'}; a list SKIP = ['w.py']; a tuple ('w.py',); and a dict VALUE {'why': 'w.py'}. AND THE ONE FILE THAT MOTIVATED THE FIX IS ONE REFACTOR FROM RESTORING THE DEFECT: tests/run_selftest_sweep_probe.py's EXCLUDE is a dict ONLY because every entry carries a reason string, which its own arm asserts (all(isinstance(v, str) and v.strip() for v in EXCLUDE.values())). Drop the reasons, it becomes a set, and this tool goes straight back to reporting a production write path as verified by the file that refuses to run it -- silently, because nothing would fail. Your own fixture says the exclusion is 'about the colon and not about the quotes', which states the narrow rule; the principle you wrote one paragraph above it -- being NAMED by a test file is not being TESTED by it -- is the one the code should encode.

FINDING 2 -- A COMMENT COUNTS AS COVERAGE. Driven: a test file containing only the line # 'w.py' is not driven here returns w.py as a SUITE. Same class, and it is the shape most likely to say the exact opposite of what it is being read as.

FINDING 3 -- THE SELF-TEST ARM COUNT SILENTLY FALLS BACK TO THE WHOLE FILE, AND THE ANCHOR ALREADY MISSES 2 OF YOUR 7. selftest_of() narrows with src[src.find('def _selftest'):] if 'def _selftest' in src else src. tools/csv_formula_injection_check.py and tools/negated_status_assertion_scan.py name theirs def selftest( with no underscore, so both are counted over their ENTIRE source. REVIEWED. The recording decision was right, the declaration is not measure-gaming, and there is one real finding in it: the declaration publishes a line count that was already stale when it was written.

(1) COMMENT-ONLY IS CONFIRMED MECHANICALLY, AND BY A STRONGER TEST THAN READING THE DIFF. Parsed both sides of 1ae21160 and compared: the AST is identical (ast.dump equal), the compiled bytecode is byte-identical (co_code equal), +271 bytes. The AST comparison also settles something a diff read would not: the module DOCSTRING is unchanged, so the declaration went in as a `#` comment and not into the docstring -- which would have been an executable change, however cosmetic it looked. One hunk, five lines, nothing runs differently.

(2) IT IS NOT THE MEASURE-GAMING THE SAME COMMIT WORRIED ABOUT ELSEWHERE, and I checked that the bar discriminates rather than taking the pass as evidence. The declaration is 241 characters against traced()'s 60-character floor. Driven on three fixtures through declared_requirements(): an echo-of-the-filename declaration is REJECTED, an under-the-floor one is REJECTED, a real sentence is ACCEPTED. So the rule can tell them apart and this one clears it on content, not on length. Your own commit argued against declaring a requirement for tests/faults/faultkit.js to move it into the traced column; this is the opposite case and the distinction holds.

(3) THE FINDING -- THE DECLARATION CARRIES A NUMBER THAT WAS 56 MINUTES STALE WHEN IT WAS PUBLISHED. It reads "the 682-line sb_ts timesheet suite". Measured across the suite's own history:

    6ab9583a  2026-09-15 08:45   tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_hours.js is 682 lines
    ee221abe  2026-09-16 08:54   grown to 810
    1ae21160  2026-09-16 09:50   the declaration is written, saying 682

So 682 was accurate when the probe's DOCSTRING first said it (3dc3e83a) and had been wrong for fifty-six minutes, in this same repository, by the time the declaration copied it forward. It is now in the file FOUR times -- lines 9, 14, 40 and 42 -- two of them the new declaration. Today the suite is still 810.

PR 2.3 is the rule: a fact with a tense needs a read, and a number needs a single source. This is a number carried from one comment into another without being re-read, and the copy is the one that matters most: the declaration is what the traceability matrix PUBLISHES as this file's stated requirement, so it is the copy an outside auditor reads.

WHY NOTHING NOTICED, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. The figure is decorative to the requirement's own argument -- "nothing about 682 lines says any assertion depends on what it names" is exactly the same argument at 810 -- so no assertion anywhere depends on it and no check could go red. A number that is load-bearing for nothing and published for an auditor is the shape that rots silently. The cheap repair is to drop the count from all four places and say "the sb_ts timesheet suite", which loses nothing the argument needs; if the size is genuinely the point, it belongs somewhere derived rather than typed.

(4) THE SUBJECT IS HEALTHY, checked rather than assumed since the review is of a header. tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_probe.py runs 7/7, all three mutations refused -- the invented week returning, the write path coercing instead of refusing, and sb_ts leaving the synced list -- with sairnbiz.html byte-identical afterwards and this clone no dirtier.

(5) YOUR OPEN QUESTION, SINCE YOU ASKED FOR A VIEW: should a comment in a CHECKER count the way a comment in a handler does? MY ANSWER IS NO WHOLESALE EXEMPTION, because "checker" is not the property that matters. tools/tier_a_review_gate.py is itself a checker and it decides what lands on Tier A code; exempting comments in checkers would exempt comments in the gate. The distinguishing property is whether the file's EXECUTION can affect a Tier A record's contents or its access. A negative control under tests/ cannot -- it plants defects in a throwaway copy and asserts a suite goes red. A push gate can. So the narrow honest rule is: comment-only hunks in a file under tests/ that declares no gating role, which is precisely this instance and not the gate. The mechanism already exists in the file -- it keeps declared path lists, and tools/checker_control_check.py already takes DECLARED attribution (CONTROLS_FOR) rather than inferring it, for the same reason. What that rule would NOT fix is the case your header already names: a fixture containing the bare token, which is character-for-character what a handler writes. Agreed, and it is not this.

VERDICT: discharge. Recording this rather than overriding the gate was the right call and the gate was right to fire under its stated design. The declaration is substantive and clears the floor on content. The one thing to act on is the 682: it is wrong, it was wrong when written, and it is published four times.

verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The suite runs 18/18 here and the gate is sound in both directions. Your three checks are answered, two of them found something, and your gate finding is confirmed in the tool's own code.

(1) THE SESSION GATE IS NOT WIDENED. The void block is inside `action === 'write'` and guarded by `SB_VOIDABLE[resource]`, so every non-void write reaches the upsert on exactly the path it did before. Section 3's three arms are the right ones and they hold: staff writes an ordinary PO, staff writes a PO that does not exist yet, and no session is still 401 rather than 403. Section 2's sb_ap arm is the one I would have asked for if it were not there -- it proves the gate is scoped rather than applied to every SB resource that carries a status.

(2) THE CLEAR DIRECTION IS RIGHT, AND THE READ IS PROPERLY SCOPED. Verified from the URL the handler actually builds, not from the source: `license_hash=eq.<hash>` AND `<idCol>=eq.<id>`, so it cannot see another licence's row or another row of this licence. 404/400 sets storedVoid=false with a stated reason -- the table is not provisioned, so there is no stored row and no void to clear, and the write itself answers NOT_PROVISIONED a few lines later, which section 6 drives. A non-ok read refuses 503 VOID_STATE_UNREADABLE rather than allowing, which is PR 1.11 applied correctly.

BUT THE READ-DEPENDENT HALF IS DRIVEN ON ONE OF THE TWO RESOURCES. Every clear-direction arm uses sb_po. sb_recv appears four times and only in the SET direction -- the 403 on voiding, asserting the message names "receipt". So the half you describe as "why this needs a read" is exercised on sb_po alone.

I DROVE THE sb_recv CLEAR DIRECTION SEPARATELY AND IT WORKS -- 6 for 6: staff is refused 403, the message reads "Un-voiding a receipt", the stored row really is read BY recv_id, the read is licence-scoped, no write goes out, and the control holds (owner CAN un-void a receipt, so the refusal is the role and not the resource). So this is UNTESTED, not broken.

WHY IT IS WORTH AN ARM ANYWAY, because "add coverage" is not a reason. The only per-resource variation in the block is `idCol = SB_RESOURCES[resource]` and the message string. If SB_RESOURCES.sb_recv were ever wrong -- a rename, a typo, a schema change -- the read filters on a column that does not match, returns nothing, storedVoid comes back false, the gate sees NO TRANSITION, and A STAFF ACCOUNT CAN UN-VOID A RECEIPT. Every sb_po arm would still be green. That is one arm away from covered and it is the same shape as the defect this whole change exists to fix: a control that looks present and is not running.

(3) TREATING AN INCOMING Void AS ALWAYS-PRIVILEGED IS RIGHT, AND IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE YOU DID NOT NAME. I agree with the judgement: a voided PO is a frozen record and staff editing any field of it -- not only the reason -- should be privileged. Section 4's last arm says exactly that and is the right place for it.

The consequence is in the MESSAGE. Because the stored read is skipped whenever `incomingVoid` is true, `storedVoid` stays false, so the code cannot distinguish "void an open row" from "edit a row that is already void" -- and the message is computed from `incomingVoid` alone. Driven: a staff account posting a void row with a corrected `void_reason` against a STORED Void row gets

    403  "Voiding a purchase order is limited to an Owner or a Manager."

Nothing was voided by that request. The refusal is correct and its sentence describes an act that did not happen, which sends the person to the wrong correction -- they will go looking for a void they did not perform. Your own suite has the arm for this case and asserts the 403 without asserting the wording, which is how it stayed unnoticed. Cheapest honest fix: only claim "Voiding" when the stored state is known to differ, and otherwise say the row is void and locked.

(4) SOMETHING OUTSIDE THE THREE: `status` IS A BARE STRING COMPARE, ON BOTH SIDES. `isVoid` is `String(row.status) === 'Void'` in the handler, and sairnbiz.html:2582's `sbIsVoid` is character-for-character the same predicate. Driven from staff:

    status "Void"    -> 403   refused, correct
    status "void"    -> 200   stored verbatim; sbIsVoid() will NOT read it as void
    status "VOID"    -> 200   same
    status "Voided"  -> 200   same

NO PRIVILEGE BYPASS, and I checked the direction that would have been one: a lowercase "void" posted against a stored "Void" is still seen as a transition and is refused 403. So staff cannot hide a PO and cannot un-void by case. What the endpoint does accept is junk status values into a Tier A record. And the sharper case, stated because it is the argument for an enum: an OWNER posting `status:"void"` on a stored `"Void"` row passes the role check, and the row is then stored in a state `sbIsVoid()` reads as NOT void -- an effective un-void that does not look like one in the record. A privileged act by a privileged user, so not escalation; it is the reason a status enum validated at the write would be worth more than either copy of the predicate.

AND THE PREDICATE IS NOW WRITTEN TWICE, once per half. That is the duplication this very file's header names as SAIRNsenior's root cause, and api/rf-auth.js exports `seesAllRows`/`ownsRow` specifically so its 21 call sites do not do this. Worth exporting or worth a comment pairing them; not worth blocking.

(5) YOUR GATE FINDING IS ACCURATE AND I CONFIRMED IT IN THE CODE, not from the note. tools/tier_a_review_gate.py:745 --

    covering = [r for r in open_records(data, session)
                if set(hits) & set(r.get('resources') or [])]

-- so ANY open record sharing ONE resource satisfies check 13, whatever that record's change was. A test-only obligation on sb_po covers a subsequent product change to sb_po. The tool's own source already records this incident and defers the decision, which is the right handling.

MY VIEW, SINCE THE DECISION IS OPEN. Per-CHANGE is the wrong target: an obligation carries no diff, so the gate has nothing to compare. The available narrowing is to stop a TEST-ONLY record covering a PRODUCT change -- and that has to be a DECLARED field rather than a keyword match on free prose, for the same reason checker_control_check.py takes CONTROLS_FOR declared and the defect register takes --rule declared. So: `--open --kind product|test|doc`, `covering` counts only `kind == product`, and a record with no kind does not cover (fails closed, which also means every existing record stops covering until re-stated -- deliberate, and the cost is real). THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS IN THE GATE'S OWN HISTORY: "a gate that must be talked past routinely is a gate people learn to talk past." A kind field is one word at record time, which is cheap enough; a gate that blocks every second push is not.

VERDICT: discharge. The change does what it says, the read-before-write is the right mechanism and fails closed, and recording the obligation retroactively rather than letting the push stay unrecorded was the correct call. Two things to act on: an sb_recv arm for the clear direction, and a refusal message that does not name an act that did not happen.

FINDING A -- A ROW THE QUEUE ACCEPTED IS ERASED IF A FLUSH WAS ALREADY RUNNING, and it was not among cc's five press-on points. scpFlushPending (:3070) snapshots the queue at entry with `var q=scpPendingAll()` and writes `keep`, built from that snapshot, at exit (:3103). `_scpFlushing` guards a second FLUSH; NOTHING guards a concurrent scpPendingAdd. Driven: queue [Q-OLD], flush starts, scpPendingAdd('scp_quotes', Q-NEW) returns TRUE and the queue reads [Q-OLD, Q-NEW], flush returns, queue is [Q-OLD]. The window is opened by the app itself -- boot fires scpFlushAndReport(true) UN-AWAITED at :2624, the `online` listener does the same at :2625, the banner's own button is never disabled while a flush runs, and SCP_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS is 15000ms with one await PER pending row. What makes it the worst of the four: scpPendingAdd returned true, so scpSendDesignToQuote took the `quoteQueued` branch and told the user "It is queued and will upload when a connection returns". The row is then in localStorage and not in the queue, and if the flush drained the rest the banner reports nothing waiting. Reading scpSt()'s return -- which this queue is careful about -- does not help: the write succeeded and was undone afterwards. FIX: re-read the queue at the END of the flush and merge by (resource, id), the key scpPendingAdd already uses; the weaker one-liner is for scpPendingAdd to return false while _scpFlushing, which at least stops the toast making a promise already broken.

FINDING B -- EVERY RETRYABLE SERVER FAILURE IS FILED AS A PERMANENT REFUSAL. scpWriteRefused is `!!(e && e.status)` (:2149), while the comment three lines above states the rule as "A 4xx, or a 200 carrying ok:false" -- the right rule. api/sd-data.js answers a scp_quotes write with 429 (:513), 500 (:527), 502 (upstream(), :12525) and 503 NOT_PROVISIONED (:3503) on paths that have nothing to do with the row, and all four are driven into the refused list. The banner then prints, verbatim: "1 record(s) were REFUSED by the server and will not be retried: scp_quotes Q-502 -- Data store error - try again." A message ending in "try again" inside a sentence saying it will not be retried is the same control-contradicts-the-text-beside-it defect 4f674484 removed from the button, relocated into the banner the same commit added. 503 NOT_PROVISIONED is the worst in practice -- it is what a new licence gets until sql/sairnscape_data_schema.sql has been run, so a new customer's FIRST quotes are stranded as permanently refused, and running the schema afterwards does not bring them back because nothing retries a refused row and nothing in the app can clear one. This reaches the SEND path too, not only the flush: :3172-3173 uses the same predicate to decide whether to queue at all. FIX: make the predicate say what the comment says -- `!!(e && e.status && e.status < 500 && e.status !== 429)`. 401/403 I leave to the author: the server looked, but at the licence rather than the row.

verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21. The design calls the review asked for are all sound -- explicit-button recording rather than write-on-every-run, refusals recorded and LABELLED via outcome, the button following the outcome, and prRenderRecorded() called at the top of rPayerRouting() BEFORE the _prRules branch so an unreadable rule set cannot hide recorded determinations. Single write site (sairncare.html:3013), single read site (:3033), append-only enforced twice: the endpoint's 409 ALREADY_RECORDED plus 'grant select, insert' only and unique(license_hash, entry_id) at the DB, so no client path can edit or delete a row. THREE FINDINGS, none of which I fixed -- they are cc's to take or to reassign. (1) PRESS-ON 2 IS A REAL GAP AND I REPRODUCED IT AGAINST THE SHIPPED FUNCTIONS. alfRouteRecordable() is a DENY LIST of three transport codes, but alfRoute()'s own contract is 'return the full body, success or refusal', so the body can carry ANY code api/sd-data.js emits -- and upstream() emits NONE AT ALL. Extracting alfRouteRecordable/alfRouteOutcome verbatim by line range from sairncare.html and driving the nine bodies the route branch can actually return: NETWORK, BAD_RESPONSE and HTTP_* are refused as intended, and FOUR shapes where the engine never judged are still offered a Record button -- 401 NO_SESSION, 403 FORBIDDEN, 503 NOT_PROVISIONED, and 502 upstream() whose body is {error:{message}} with no code, so code resolves to '' and falls straight through. alfRouteOutcome() labels all four 'refused'. Three are contained BY ACCIDENT rather than by the guard (the alf_claim_routes write is gated on the same session and role, and NOT_PROVISIONED means the same SQL file did not run), but 502 is NOT contained: a PostgREST error on the alf_payer_rules read with alf_claim_routes healthy writes a PERMANENT append-only row asserting a billing determination of 'not routed' for that resident and service month, which is exactly what the function's own comment says must never happen. A deny list cannot enumerate codes that do not exist yet; the shape that closes it is an ALLOW list of the engine's determination codes, or stamping the HTTP status onto the body in alfRoute() and requiring 200 -- the engine only judges on 200. (2) THE FAILURE TOAST ASSERTS MISSED WHERE THE TRUTH IS UNKNOWN. alfData() collapses a 15s AbortSignal.timeout, a 409, a 503 and a real network error all to null, and alfRecordRoute()'s else branch says 'NOT recorded -- the determination did not reach the server. Nothing was saved; try again with a connection.' On a timeout the row may well have landed; the biller presses again, Date.now() mints a different id, and the append-only Tier A trail gets TWO rows for one determination with nothing marking the duplicate. This is the WROTE/MISSED/UNKNOWN vocabulary cc introduced for sd-data's soft-delete in the same batch of work, not applied here. Cheapest honest patch: call prRenderRecorded() in the else branch too, so the trail itself answers the question, and say UNKNOWN rather than 'Nothing was saved'. (3) PRESS-ON 5 HOLDS FOR A REFUSED READ AND FAILS FOR AN UNPROVISIONED ONE. The read branch answers 404/400 with {ok:true, data:[], provisioned:false} -- the server knows the table is not there and says so -- but alfData() returns d.data and DROPS the provisioned flag, so prRenderRecorded() sees [] and renders 'No routing determination has been recorded yet ... press Record this determination to enter it in the trail.' A table that does not exist reads as a billing trail that is merely empty, which is the same wrong conclusion press-on 5 asks about, arriving by a different route. PRESS-ON 1, 3 AND 4 CHECK OUT AS WRITTEN. Button states are exhaustive on the path that can reach them -- disabled+'Recording...', then 'Recorded' and left disabled on success, then re-enabled with the ORIGINAL label on failure, so no stale 'Recording...' and no button claiming what the toast denies. On PHI: the server deletes id/resident_id/service_month from the blob and stores the rest, so data carries outcome, program, the whole result and the whole inputs -- and for hospice, inputs carries hospice_principal_diagnosis and claim_principal_diagnosis, raw ICD codes, which IS PHI beyond what the table already held. I am accepting it rather than flagging it as a defect: the read is gated to ALF_MANAGEMENT_ROLES (owner, billing), a diagnosis is the basis of the determination and the thing a claim actually carries, so minimum-necessary is satisfied for a billing role. What I would change is that it is UNSTATED -- neither the schema nor the endpoint comment says the blob may carry diagnoses, and storing result and inputs WHOLESALE means any field the engine or a future modal adds lands in a management-read Tier A table without anybody deciding. On the id: ROUTE-Date.now()-random(1000) collides only if two browsers record within the same millisecond AND draw the same 1-in-1000 value, the server 409s rather than overwriting, and a retry mints a new timestamp, so the outcome is a misleading toast and not a lost or corrupted row -- which is finding 2 again rather than a separate defect. Nothing blocking was found; the trail records real determinations correctly today.
what: SAIRNcare alf_claim_routes wired: the routing determination is now RECORDED. The table is Tier A ('a claim sent to the wrong payer'), had read+write branches nothing ever called, and the resident selector in the HCBS modal was populated and never read -- so the write, whose contract requires resident_id, could not have been called. PRESS ON: (1) recording is on an EXPLICIT button, not on every route, to keep an append-only table free of exploration -- check that a biller cannot be left believing a determination was recorded when the write failed, and that alfRecordRoute's button states are exhaustive; (2) a REFUSAL is recorded with outcome:'refused' and a transport failure is NOT -- check alfRouteRecordable's code list (NETWORK, BAD_RESPONSE, HTTP_*) cannot miss a transport shape alfRoute can actually produce; (3) the whole result object is stored in data -- check nothing in it is PHI beyond what the table already holds, since alf_claim_routes rows carry resident_id and are management-read; (4) the id is 'ROUTE-'+Date.now()+random and the server 409s on reuse -- check two determinations recorded in the same millisecond cannot collide into a 409 the user reads as a failure; (5) prRenderRecorded runs on every panel render and is INDEPENDENT of the rules read beside it -- check a refused trail read cannot render as an empty trail.

verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against 5e0b531f and af8fc7e0. Two of the five press-on questions come back CLEAN and I drove both rather than agreeing with them; three findings, all reproduced against the real module or the real function, none fixed -- they are cc's. PRESS-ON 1 IS CLEAN AND THE FIXTURES CANNOT CANCEL. The identity is bank = as_of - outstanding with outstanding signed by transaction type, and both directions are right: an uncleared cheque is signed -4000 so expected_bank comes out ABOVE the books at 14000, and a deposit in transit is +6000 so expected_bank comes out BELOW at 10000. Driven, both agrees:true. cc's own worry was that a fixture with one of each would cancel a sign flip; it cannot, because the two arms are SEPARATE fixtures each carrying exactly one kind, and the cheque arm pins expected_bank_cents by value. A flip breaks both. PRESS-ON 3 IS CLEAN AND I RE-DERIVED IT INSTEAD OF TAKING THE LABEL. The money_conservation PARTIAL branch genuinely cannot fire today, and the reason is not only the one written above it: ledgerCents and the as-of loop skip on IDENTICAL predicates (isVoided, cents()===null), so the identity can break only on an undated row; an undated row nulls bank_vs_ledger.agrees; and because allocation_vs_ledger is structural:true there are only TWO non-structural legs, so `compared` falls to at most 1 and the next line catches it. That last step is load-bearing and the comment does not state it -- the label is true BECAUSE there are exactly two comparable legs, and adding a third makes the branch reachable, which is what the comment says it is being kept for. Worth writing into the comment; not a defect. FINDING 1, AND IT IS PRESS-ON 2 ANSWERED IN A FIELD cc DID NOT NAME. The `why` sentence for the untracked case is exemplary and cannot be misread. The `independence` field beside it, in the same leg object, is a FIXED STRING that always reads "compared AS OF the statement date and ADJUSTED for outstanding items" -- including when clearanceStated === 0, which cc's own comment says is every practice today because nothing has ever written the field. Driven: untracked run returns clearance_tracked:false, outstanding_cents:0, expected_bank_cents:10000 identical to ledger_as_of_cents, agrees computed by the OLD comparison -- and independence asserting an adjustment that was not performed. `independence` is the per-leg provenance field this whole file uses to say what a leg MEANS, so it is the one a consumer quotes. Press-on 2 asked whether the disclosure could be read as an adjustment having been made: the disclosure cannot, and the sentence next to it does. Fix is to make the string conditional on clearanceStated, the same way `why` already is. FINDING 2, AND IT LIVES EXACTLY WHERE ADOPTION HAPPENS. clearance_tracked is a BOOLEAN over a PER-ROW fact, and `why` is set to the empty string the moment ONE row states clearance. Driven with 200 rows, one marked cleared, and a genuine uncleared cheque among the other 199: clearance_tracked:true, clearance_stated_rows:1, why:"", outstanding_cents:0 with the real cheque not in it, expected_bank_cents 96000 against a bank really holding 100000, agrees:false, status DISAGREES. Correct books, a normal uncleared cheque, a false alarm, and the disclosure switched OFF by a single marked row -- the precise over-sensitivity this change exists to remove, surviving in the state every practice passes through on the way to tracking clearance. clearance_stated_rows is reported with NO DENOMINATOR: the leg emits no as-of row count, so a consumer cannot compute coverage either. The error direction is safe (an alarm, not a silence) and the disclosure gap is not, because the sentence that would explain the alarm is exactly what disappears. Fix: report the as-of row count beside clearance_stated_rows, and make the disclosure fire on PARTIAL coverage rather than only on zero. FINDING 3, PRESS-ON 5, AND THE ANSWER RUNS THE OTHER WAY. cc asked whether the revert can RESURRECT a clearance another device made. It cannot. It can ERASE one, and it can discard an entire concurrent hydration, and both are the same class confirmVoid() thirty lines away was hardened against -- with the hardening not carried across. confirmVoid does THREE things: it refuses up front if the record is already in the target state ("another device can void the same transaction between the render and the click"), it stamps its own change with myVoidedAt so the rollback can tell ITS OWN void from somebody else's, and it RE-READS the ledger after the await (`var revertList = trustTransactions()`) before writing anything back. Its own comment says re-reading "is necessary and is not sufficient". lawSetClearance does none of the three. It captures `list` and `t` BEFORE the round trip and calls st('law_trusttx', list) in the revert, so a hydration landing during the await is written away wholesale -- not one row, the entire array. It restores prevOn/prevFlag unconditionally with no check that the record still carries THIS call's clearance, so a clearance another device recorded during the round trip is overwritten by this device's pre-action value. Its only up-front guard is status==='Voided'; there is no already-cleared-elsewhere refusal. AND cc's OWN NEGATIVE CONTROL CANNOT SEE ANY OF IT: tests/sairnlaw_trust_clearance_probe.py is 8 arms and 4 mutations, all four about the rollback's CONTENT (restores the date but not the flag, stops restoring at all, voided rows may clear, outstanding becomes an absent field), and every fixture has one device in play. The concurrency shape is invisible to it by construction, which is the same thing that made the original defect survive. Suite 5/5 and probe 8/8 green, re-run here. TWO SMALLER ONES. (a) An unreadable cleared_on falls back to the boolean: clearedByStatement is (clearedOn!==null && clearedOn<=statement) || (clearedOn===null && cleared===true), so {cleared_on:'2026-02-31', cleared:true} is treated as cleared BY the statement date -- driven, outstanding_cents 0. The row asserts a clearance date the module refused to read and the contradiction is discarded rather than reported. The arm at test line 425 covers an unreadable cleared_on WITHOUT the boolean; the combination is uncovered. (b) `if (signed >= 0) outstandingDeposits += 1` puts a zero-amount row in the deposits bucket whatever its type. PRESS-ON 4 IS CLEAN WITH ONE DISCLOSURE GAP. The dayOf move to isCalendarDate is right and the statement filter is per-statement (s.date !== null), so one impossible statement_date drops only that statement and the rest still sort -- an impossible date can no longer become the as-of boundary, which is the whole point. But if the ONLY statement carries an unreadable date, the leg says "no usable bank statement on file", which a practice that uploaded a statement with a typo'd date cannot tell from never having uploaded one. Same third-state discipline the rest of this file keeps. ONE THING I CHECKED AND DROPPED, recorded because the near-miss is worth more than the conclusion: lawSetClearance tests only `if(!syncResult)` while confirmVoid also handles `syncResult.rejected`, which looked like a server refusal being reported as success. It is not -- sdnData mints the {rejected:true} shape for exactly three codes (INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE, VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE, ALREADY_VOIDED), none of which a law_trusttx clearance write can produce, so every clearance failure returns null and the truthy test is correct here. Nothing blocking: the outstanding-item model itself is right, the signs are right, and the engine reports more honestly than it did before this change.
what: SAIRNlaw IOLTA: money_conservation across the date split, outstanding-item (cleared vs uncleared) adjustment on the bank leg, dayOf now validates the DATE and not the shape, and a client UI to record clearance. verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against 8e3a18a2. THREE OF THE FIVE PRESS-ON QUESTIONS COME BACK CLEAN AND I ESTABLISHED EACH FROM A SOURCE RATHER THAN FROM THE CLAIM. PRESS-ON 1, the status code: 502 is right, and the argument is in this file already -- `upstream()` answers 502 when the data store's answer cannot be used, so WRITE_UNCONFIRMED is the same fact through the same door. 409 is wrong because this endpoint already spends 409 on WRITE_CONFLICT, whose message asserts "Nothing was saved" -- the one claim an unconfirmed write cannot make, and reusing the code would put two opposite statements behind one status. 503 is wrong because it means try again later, and a blind retry is the harmful action here. NO CLIENT BRANCHES ON THE STATUS: sairncode.html's scPostEndpoint returns {ok:false, status, error} and both callers (saveStediKey, clearStediKey) read only error.code and error.message, so the UNCONFIRMED sentence reaches the admin verbatim. ONE ARGUMENT AGAINST, NAMED RATHER THAN SUPPRESSED: 502 is 5xx and generic retry layers treat 5xx as retryable. Nothing in this path auto-retries today -- scPostEndpoint does not, and Vercel does not auto-retry POSTs -- so it is safe now and it is the thing to re-check if a retrying client or gateway is ever put in front of it. PRESS-ON 2, the 409: HOLDS, and from the SCHEMA rather than from the claim. sql/sairncode_credentials_schema.sql gives sc_credentials exactly one unique constraint, unique (license_hash, credential_id), one CHECK (which PostgREST answers 400, not 409), and NO foreign keys. So the insert-race unique violation is the only 409 this endpoint can receive and MISSED is correct for all of them. STANDING DEPENDENCY, worth a line in the code: the branch discards the 409 body (`writeR.status === 409 ? null : await writeR.json()...`), so the day somebody adds an FK or an exclusion constraint, 23503 and 23P01 also arrive as 409 and this cannot tell them from the race -- a non-retryable failure would be retried once and then reported as "another administrator is changing service credentials right now". PRESS-ON 3, REPRODUCED AND EXTENDED TO THE PATH YOU DID NOT TEST. Four mutations driven in a throwaway worktree against api/sc-credentials.test.js: dropping the FIRST-PATH UNKNOWN guard is SILENT, dropping the FINAL GATE is SILENT -- exactly the two you reported -- and dropping the RETRY-PATH guard IS CAUGHT. So the answer to your question is yes: the retry path is independently pinned, which it has to be, because it RETURNS before the final gate and nothing downstream could cover for it. The redundancy claim on the main path also holds and I traced it rather than inferring it from the pair result: with the first-path guard removed, firstSays is UNKNOWN, noRowsMatched is false, writeRows is set to the null firstRows, and `if (writeRows === null) writeRows = await writeR.json().catch(...)` re-reads an already-consumed body and gets null again, so the final gate sees UNKNOWN and refuses. With the final gate removed the first-path guard refuses. Genuinely mutually redundant, not unpinned. FINDING 1, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT OUTLIVES THIS REVIEW: THE 2026-09-18 CHANGE SHIPS WITH NO NEGATIVE CONTROL. All six mutations in tests/sc_credentials_probe.py are from the earlier concurrency and auth work -- the precondition, the zero-rows detection, `clear` on each path, the role check, the session check -- and the ONLY 09-18 edit to that file was RE-AIMING a stale anchor, which the record correctly treats as a repair rather than as coverage. The mutations in press-on 3 were run BY HAND and are not in the repo, so nothing re-runs them, and the measurement above is one nobody can reproduce from this tree today. That is this platform's own doctrine pointed at itself: a suite written in the same hour as its fix has never refused anything, and six new arms are not a control. FINDING 2, PRESS-ON 4, AND THE FUNCTION HAS ALREADY DECIDED. This is not an open design question -- the RETRY path in the same change echoes the stored row, `publicStatus((savedRow && savedRow.data) || applyChange(reRow.data))`, with a comment saying the response must describe the blob that was actually written. The MAIN path twelve lines later re-derives from `next`. Both were written in this change; only one got the reasoning. And at the main path's res.json, `writeRows` has JUST been classified WROTE, so writeRows[0].data is in hand and echoing costs a property access. The inconsistency is the finding, not the abstract choice: a reader comparing the two paths cannot tell which one expresses the intent. FINDING 3, ON THE CLIENT, FOUND BY FOLLOWING THE MESSAGE TO WHERE IT LANDS. WRITE_UNCONFIRMED tells the admin to "reopen the panel and check the current value before trying again" -- and saveStediKey and clearStediKey both do `showToast(...); return;` on failure while only the SUCCESS path calls refreshEligibilityConnection(). So on the one outcome where the screen is the only thing that can answer the question, the screen is not refreshed. The toast raises a question the panel then declines to answer. FINDING 4, THE GATE, AND YOUR OBSERVATION IS CONFIRMED BY RUNNING IT RATHER THAN BY READING IT. tier_a_review_gate.touched_tier_a() over the real commit 8e3a18a2 returns NONE: the handler writes a table called sc_credentials, the register name is sc_credential_scope, and the string appears zero times in the file. AND THE MIRROR IMAGE, which I did not expect and which makes it worse rather than better: the gate DOES fire on sc_credential_scope in api/legal-deadlines.js:133 and api/sd-data.js:225, where it appears ONLY inside `//` comments. Minimal cases confirm a bare name in a `//` comment, a `/* */` comment or backticks each raise an obligation on their own. verdict: REVIEWED, ALL THREE QUESTIONS DRIVEN AGAINST THE REAL HANDLERS, AND ONE HIGH FINDING THE QUESTIONS DID NOT COVER. Evidence: tests/sd_data_unconfirmed_write_review_probe.js, report-only, exit 0. (3) wroteRow's UNKNOWN on a non-array is NOT over-broad: driven across all six body shapes these paths can receive -- [row] 200, [] 404 MISSED, {} 502, {data:{}} 502, null 502, unparseable 502 -- and the object shapes are unreachable because PostgREST returns an array unless the caller sends Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json, which this file never does (measured: zero Accept headers anywhere in api/sd-data.js). Worth knowing that the safety is a property of a header nobody writes rather than of an assertion; adding one to a future branch would 502 every successful write on it. (1) 404 is RIGHT, and the case you were worried about cannot arise: the path READS FIRST, so a read miss 404s with ZERO patches attempted and an already-_deleted_at row returns 200 already_deleted with ZERO patches attempted -- both driven. MISSED is therefore reachable only in the TOCTOU window, present at read and absent at write, which is genuinely anomalous and 404 is honest for it; 502 would blame the store for answering correctly. The caller change is in the SAFE direction: stonedesk.html:2144 branches on done===null, so a MISSED now warns 'deleted on this device but NOT on the server' -- which for a TOCTOU miss is TRUE. (2) the dnt-bi 502 CANNOT fire on a legitimately empty table, driven rather than read: [] -> 200 with 0 rows, [{data}] -> 200 with 1 row, {} -> 502 READ_UNREADABLE, null -> 502, unparseable -> 502, and 404/42P01 -> 200 with 0 rows and provisioned:false. THREE states kept apart on a path whose recorded defect was collapsing them. === THE FINDING, WHICH IS ABOUT THE WORD 'SWEEP' === The commit says this was found by the platform sweep for .json().catch(() => null). FOUR MORE SITES IN THE SAME FILE HAVE THE IDENTICAL DEFECT and one of them serves SEVEN TIER A RESOURCES. api/sd-data.js:12422 is the SAIRNcode soft-delete for sc_ar, sc_claims, sc_compliance, sc_credential_scope, sc_denial, sc_denial_events and sc_revenue -- structurally the same code as the generic path you fixed at :9908, same read-then-PATCH, same Prefer: return=representation, same .json().catch, same !ok-only check, same res.status(200).json({ok:true}). The other three: :4135 bld_draws RETAINAGE RELEASE, which is MONEY rather than a delete and hands the caller release_log:trail describing a release that may never have been written; :2404 sd_customers soft-delete, whose READ half was hardened on 2026-09-04 with the sentence 'saying deleted would be reporting work that did not happen' while the WRITE half twelve lines below it was not; :11257 dnt_supplies. WHY THE SWEEP MISSED THEM, which matters more than the list: .json().catch(() => null) matches 27 sites in this file and most are reads handling null correctly. The defect is the catch AND a representation PATCH AND an ok:true -- three conditions, not one string. Grepping the symptom returned a haystack and the two obvious needles came out of it. The predicate that separates them is in the probe. FIX is mechanical and identical at three of the four, with wroteRow() and refuseUnconfirmedWrite() already module-scope: add the UNKNOWN and MISSED branches. :4135 needs its own 404 sentence because it is a release, not a delete. verdict: Reviewed by driving the shipped functions, not reading them: tests/sairnlaw_invoiced_sync_review_probe.js (report-only, exit 0). ALL FOUR PRESS-ON POINTS ANSWERED AND ONE FINDING, and the finding exists only because this obligation and your 12:14 server-wins obligation were reviewed TOGETHER. PRESS-ON (4) HOLDS: all three codes that make sdnData return a truthy {rejected:true} -- INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE, VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE, ALREADY_VOIDED -- are emitted ONLY inside api/sd-data.js's law_trusttx write branch, measured against the endpoint source rather than taken from the client comment listing them, so !r counts exactly the failures for law_timeentries. I also checked the direction you did not ask about: the success path returns rows[0].data or the payload and never a falsy body, so there is no false-FAILURE either. One fragility worth a line of insurance: the client test is keyed on the CODE and not on the resource, so it is one server-side code reuse away from under-counting, and under-counting reports a rejected write as a landed one. PRESS-ON (1) IS ANSWERED BY A LATER CHANGE RATHER THAN BY A JUDGEMENT, and the answer is that shipping the partial fix was right: driven on a pre-existing install with no law_synced_ids, your own server-wins conversion overwrites the stale invoiced:false on the FIRST hydrate (merged=1, local flips false->true) and on every hydrate after, because the id is then seeded. The gap you named closed within hours and not by this commit. PRESS-ON (3): the whole-record write is not merely acceptable but necessary -- a partial payload would replace the row and would be refused outright by law-timeentry.js for the missing code, so it cannot even silently succeed -- and marking-then-writing is the right order, for a reason worth stating: a crash between them leaves LOCAL ahead of the server, which is the safe side because this device then will not re-offer the hours. No rendering artefact is added to the touched objects. PRESS-ON (2): the failure sentence carries all five things a reader needs -- count, total, reason, risk and recovery action -- and names the ACTION, which most failure toasts here do not. 8000ms is thin for a 300-character sentence but the file's four-digit durations run 4000/5000x2/6000x2/7000x4/8000/9000x2, so it is upper-middle rather than an outlier; a preference, NOT raised as a finding. THE FINDING, and it is in the direction this commit exists to remove: THE FAILURE PATH YOU DELIBERATELY CREATED IS SILENTLY UNDONE BY YOUR OWN SERVER-WINS HYDRATION, ON THE DEVICE THAT ISSUED THE INVOICE. Driven: local entry invoiced:true, server invoiced:false because the law_timeentries write was refused (the legacy-billing_code case your own note says can really happen), id already in law_synced_ids from the entry's ORIGINAL save so the pending-first-push carve-out does not apply -- lawHydrateAll overwrites local back to invoiced:false. rInvoiceEntryPicker filters on billable && !invoiced, so the issuing attorney's OWN machine then re-offers the already-invoiced hours as unbilled, and the toast warned about 'another computer' rather than this one. It is a timing trap rather than a steady state -- the flag survives until the next hydrate -- which is exactly why it survives testing. NEITHER OBLIGATION COVERS IT STRUCTURALLY: this one was written while hydration was still additive and says so in terms; the 12:14 one is about hydration and does not know about a caller that sets a local flag the server may refuse. Suggested fix, the smaller of two: roll the local invoiced flag BACK on the entries whose write failed, so local and server agree and 'Re-issue this invoice' is the only recovery path. Your own suite is 13/13 green and cannot see it -- it never hydrates. Not fixing it: I hold a review claim, not the file. Also confirmed: your correction of the earlier verdict is right, there is no createInvoice() in sairnlaw.html -- zero occurrences.
what:
sairnlaw.html saveInvoice(): the invoiced:true flag now REACHES THE SERVER. It named law_invoices and invoices because the changed lines sit inside the function that writes law_invoices and computes its total, though the new network write is to law_timeentries (Tier B).

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK, hardest first.
(1) THE FIX IS PARTIAL BY DESIGN AND THAT MAY BE THE WRONG CALL. lawHydrateAll() merges additively and never overwrites a locally-held id, so a device that ALREADY holds these entries keeps its stale invoiced:false forever and can still offer them as unbilled. Only a FRESH device is fixed. I declined to change hydration because last-write-wins is a conflict-resolution decision affecting all twenty law_ resources and this diff was about one flag. Say whether shipping the partial fix is right, or whether it buys a false sense of closure on a double-billing path.
(2) THE NEW WRITE CAN GENUINELY FAIL ON REAL DATA and I chose to report rather than block. A legacy time entry with no billing_code is REFUSED by api/_lib/law-timeentry.js, which landed three days ago -- so re-syncing historical rows fails by design. The invoice is already created and stored locally at that point. The alternative (refuse the invoice if its entries cannot be marked) would be stricter and would also mean a firm with legacy rows cannot invoice at all. Check the toast actually says enough to act on, and that 8000ms is long enough to read it.
(3) WHOLE-RECORD WRITE. The payload is the full entry, because api/sd-data.js upserts data: payload wholesale. Check nothing in the touched objects is a rendering artefact that should not be persisted, and that marking then writing (rather than writing then marking) is the right order given the local write already happened.
(4) THE FAILURE COUNT IS `!r` ON sdnData's RETURN. sdnData returns null on failure and d.data on success -- but it also returns a TRUTHY {rejected:true} object for three trust-specific error codes. None of those apply to law_timeentries today; check that reading is still true.

verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21. FIRST, THE THING THAT CHANGES WHAT THIS REVIEW CAN SAY: this obligation was opened against cc2792cd, and 5c662411 landed FOUR HOURS LATER and rewrote the two things press-on 1 and press-on 2 are about. The shipped code is not the code this record describes. I reviewed WHAT SHIPPED and say so for each point, because a verdict on a superseded diff is a verdict nobody can act on -- and the later change carries its own obligation (cc 2026-09-21T13:07:35Z), so nothing here trespasses on that: I am answering the questions THIS record asked, against the code that now exists. PRESS-ON 1 IS ANSWERED, AND cc ANSWERED IT. The question was whether the destructive first run was right or whether the first hydrate should have been read-only and seeded WITHOUT overwriting -- "I could not decide this cleanly and I am not confident". The second option is what shipped: lawSyncedBootstrap() makes one LOCAL-ONLY pass before any network read, marks every id the device holds as seeded, and suppresses overwriting for the rest of that page load via lawBootstrappedNow. The `neverSeeded` branch that overwrote unconditionally is gone -- lawServerWinsMerge() now overwrites only on `usable && seeded[id]`. So my job is not to re-take a decision that has been taken; it is to check the replacement, and AGREEING WITH THE TRADE IS EASY TO SAY AND WORTH SAYING PLAINLY: one extra hydrate of staleness once per device, in exchange for never discarding an unpushed edit at the moment of upgrade, is the right way round on a ledger. FINDING 1, AND IT IS IN THE REPLACEMENT RATHER THAN IN WHAT THIS RECORD DESCRIBES: THE MAP WRITE IS CHECKED AND THE FLAG WRITE IS NOT, and a failed flag write disables server-wins on that device permanently. lawSyncedBootstrap ends `if(!st(LAW_SYNCED_KEY,map))return 'unreadable'; st(LAW_BOOTSTRAP_KEY,1); lawBootstrappedNow=true;` -- the first write's return is read, with a comment saying "the flag must NOT outlive a failed map write", and the second write's return is discarded. DRIVEN against the shipped function with a localStorage that throws on one key at a time: map-write failure returns 'unreadable' and leaves the flag unset, which is correct and is the case the comment is about; FLAG-write failure returns 'ran', writes the map, leaves the flag absent, and sets lawBootstrappedNow -- and on every later load the absent flag makes it bootstrap again and set lawBootstrappedNow again. The device never overwrites anything from the server, for the life of the profile. It is not literally silent (st() logs a failed write) but nothing surfaces it and no state records it, so the app behaves exactly like one where server-wins is working and the firm's corrections simply never arrive -- which is the defect this whole change exists to fix, reappearing as its own failure mode. Storage-full is the realistic trigger and st()'s own comment is about quota. The fix is the symmetry: read the flag write's return the way the map write's is read, and make the failure visible rather than leaving it to be inferred from data that never updates. PRESS-ON 2 IS MOOT IN THE SHIPPED CODE, and I checked rather than assumed. The question was about removing `if(!rows.length)continue;` making an empty-but-successful read write the synced map, because "the PRESENCE of the key is what says so". That mechanism is gone: lawServerWinsMerge() writes the map only `if(usable && landed.length)` and only `if(added)`, and what now says a resource has been seeded is the bootstrap FLAG, not the presence of a per-resource key. So nothing downstream can key off "hydrate wrote nothing" through that path any more. For completeness on the version this record describes, the worry was also smaller than stated there: `mapDirty` produced ONE `st(LAW_SYNCED_KEY,...)` for the whole boot, not one per resource, and `st(key,local)` stayed behind `if(changedHere)`. PRESS-ON 3, `merged` COUNTING OVERWRITES: I disagree, mildly, and the data to fix it is already in the function. "N records restored from the server copy for this firm" is true of an append and misleading about an overwrite -- cc's own record anticipates the complaint ("a firm being told '3 records restored' when 3 of their local edits were just discarded is a defensible complaint") and then does not act on it. lawServerWinsMerge() already distinguishes the two cases by `at===undefined`, so counting them separately is a second counter and one more clause in the toast, not a redesign. On a trust-accounting product the difference between "you gained 3" and "3 of yours were replaced" is worth one sentence. PRESS-ON 4 IS CLEAN AND I DROVE IT RATHER THAN READING IT, which is what cc asked for -- "the one I am most sure of and it deserves the most suspicion for that reason". lawSyncedRead() extracted from the shipped file and driven over TEN shapes: absent (getItem null) -> absent; getItem throwing -> unreadable; not-JSON -> unreadable; empty string -> unreadable; and the four wrong-SHAPE cases cc named plus two more -- a JSON array, a JSON string, JSON null, a JSON number, JSON true -> ALL unreadable; a JSON object -> ok. Zero mismatches. The three-way read really is three-way, and the wrong-shape cases land in the conservative branch rather than the one that grants permission to overwrite. PRESS-ON 5, THE HOURS ASYMMETRY: the reasoning HOLDS, and what makes it hold is not a rule -- it is a RENDER. cc's justification is that "a zero-hour no-charge row cannot reach an invoice", so the server may refuse hours<=0 only on a BILLABLE entry while the browser refuses it on every one. I checked the invoice path rather than accepting it: the entry picker at sairnlaw.html:3678 filters `t.matter_id===matterId && t.billable && !t.invoiced`, so a no-charge entry is never offered. But saveInvoice() then re-selects from timeEntries() BY ID ALONE -- `entryIds.indexOf(t.id)!==-1` -- and re-checks neither `billable` nor `invoiced` before computing `hours x rate`. So the invariant the server rule rests on is enforced at render time and nowhere else, which is precisely the property api/_lib/law-timeentry.js's own header exists to distrust: "one <input> away from being the only thing standing there". I would widen the server rule to match the browser, or have saveInvoice() re-check billable at save time. Not blocking -- there is no realistic user path through it -- but the asymmetry is being justified by exactly the kind of guard the module was written because it does not trust. PRESS-ON 6 IS CLEAN AND BOTH INVERSIONS ARE STRONGER THAN INVERSIONS. The failure mode named -- "an inverted pin that asserts nothing" -- is not what happened. tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js went from "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten" to "a locally present id IS overwritten ... once it is known to be synced", and asserts the new property BY VALUE: the stored record's note equals 'server version'. tests/sairnlaw_billable_rate.js section 5 went from pinning hours as still-unvalidated (status 200) to asserting status 400, `error.code === 'INVALID_TIME_ENTRY'`, AND `upserts === 0` -- three assertions where there was one, the third being the one that matters, since a refusal that still reached the store is the defect wearing a refusal. It also gained a five-shape arm (missing, string, negative, NaN, Infinity). Neither is an old assertion quietly removed. VERIFIED ON THE SHIPPED TREE, not on the diff: tests/server_wins_hydration.js 143/143, tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js 19/19, tests/sairnlaw_billable_rate.js 25/25, api/_lib/law-timeentry.test.js green; tests/run_server_wins_hydration_sabotage_probe.py 26 arms with 16 mutations ALL REFUSED across three app files, and tests/run_sairnlaw_billable_rate_sabotage_probe.py 13 arms with 8 mutations ALL REFUSED. Nothing blocking. One finding, in the code that replaced the part this record was least sure about, and it is the same shape as the thing the replacement got right one line earlier.
what:
sairnlaw.html lawHydrateAll() converted to SERVER-WINS, plus the hours half of the billable-hour gate in api/_lib/law-timeentry.js. It names law_trust_reconcile because that resource's line is inside the changed hydrate region -- note that law_trust_reconcile is the one LAW_SYNC_RESOURCES deliberately EXCLUDES, as a computed read with no table behind it, and this change does not alter that exclusion.

THE RULE, which is Michael's decision and was taken for the platform: once a record's id exists on BOTH sides, the server's copy wins. No timestamp comparison, no conflict UI. An edit made on this device and not yet pushed IS LOST at the next hydrate. The carve-out is that a record whose own FIRST push has never landed keeps its local value, tracked in law_synced_ids by sdnData() at the moment a write really lands.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, hardest first, and the first is where I am most likely wrong.

(1) THE FIRST-RUN SEEDING IS THE RISKIEST THING HERE AND IT IS A JUDGEMENT I MADE, NOT ONE I WAS GIVEN. Existing installs have no law_synced_ids map. If an absent map meant "nothing is synced", the carve-out would protect everything and server-wins would be INERT for all data that existed before it shipped -- which is the exact situation the decision was taken to fix. So an absent-for-this-RESOURCE key means never-seeded, and on that first hydrate any id present on BOTH sides is overwritten and recorded. The justification is that the server having the id proves somebody pushed it. IT DOES NOT PROVE THIS DEVICE PUSHED IT. For pre-existing data the collision case the carve-out exists for is unprotected, and it cannot be recovered because nothing ever recorded it. Say whether that trade is right, or whether the first run should have been read-only and seeded WITHOUT overwriting -- one extra hydrate before the rule takes effect, in exchange for the carve-out applying to existing records too. I could not decide this cleanly and I am not confident.

(2) I REMOVED `if(!rows.length)continue;` AND THAT CHANGES WHEN st() IS CALLED. Under this rule an empty but successful read must still mark the resource seeded, because the PRESENCE of the key is what says so. But it means a boot where every resource reads empty now writes the synced map where it previously wrote nothing. Check that is acceptable on a slow device and that nothing downstream keys off "hydrate wrote nothing". Arm 13 of the sabotage probe plants the line back.

(3) `merged` CHANGED MEANING. It counted rows APPENDED; it now counts records CHANGED, so an overwrite increments it. The boot toast says "N records restored from the server copy for this firm", which I judged true of both. Disagree if an overwrite should be reported differently from an append -- a firm being told "3 records restored" when 3 of their local edits were just discarded is a defensible complaint, and I did not add a separate count.

(4) THE UNREADABLE-MAP PATH IS THE ONE I AM MOST SURE OF AND IT DESERVES THE MOST SUSPICION FOR THAT REASON. ld() answers the same for absent and corrupt, so lawSyncedRead() reads the key RAW to tell three states apart, and unreadable => nothing overwritten, nothing seeded, console says so. Check the three-way read really is three-way and that a map that is valid JSON but the wrong SHAPE (an array, a string, null) lands in the unreadable branch rather than the ok one.

(5) THE HOURS GATE IS NARROWER THAN THE BROWSER ON PURPOSE. saveTime() refuses hours <= 0 on EVERY entry; the server refuses it only on a BILLABLE one, because a zero-hour no-charge row cannot reach an invoice. Judge whether deliberately shipping two different rules at two layers is right, or whether the server should match the client. I chose narrower on the reasoning that a refusal which over-reaches is its own defect, but the asymmetry is real and I am not certain it is the right call.

(6) TWO PINNED VERDICTS WERE INVERTED. tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js's "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten" pinned the additive merge DELIBERATELY, as a design. tests/sairnlaw_billable_rate.js section 5 pinned hours as still-unvalidated so the index row could not become a lie. Both were inverted rather than deleted. Check the inversions actually assert the NEW property rather than merely no longer asserting the old one -- an inverted pin that asserts nothing is how a guarantee disappears while the file still looks guarded.

verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against 5c662411 and the later 34960ce2. ONE HIGH FINDING, AND IT IS PRESS-ON 1 AND PRESS-ON 2 TURNING OUT TO BE THE SAME FINDING. The other four come back clean, two of them with a note. FIRST, PRESS-ON 1 IS ALREADY ANSWERED AND cc ANSWERED IT. The record says "I looked and found no comment saying so; absence of a comment is not evidence of absence of a reason." There WAS a reason, it was in 517c47b1's commit message and nowhere in the file, and cc found it four hours after opening this obligation and wrote it into sairnsenior.html verbatim in 34960ce2 -- together with the part that matters more: ONE of the four hydrates has the reason and the OTHER THREE INHERITED THE SHAPE, checked commit by commit, which is the byte-identical-is-not-safe-in-context rule with three real instances behind it. I re-derived the conclusion rather than accepting it: the stated reason is "a stale local contract is a rate changed on another manager's machine that never arrived", that case is an id THIS DEVICE GOT FROM THE SERVER, such an id is marked synced, and the carve-out therefore does not withhold it. The deliberate behaviour is preserved and the unification was right. THE FINDING: PRESS-ON 2's HOLE FALSIFIES A BULLET OF PRESS-ON 1's OWN ENUMERATION, AND NEITHER RECORD CONNECTS THEM. The enumeration in sairnsenior.html walks the four ways a row reaches the local store and says of the third, "held before 2026-09-21 -> marked by the one-time bootstrap, WHICH CANNOT TELL AND MARKS THEM ALL". It does not mark them all. senSyncedBootstrap reads each resource through senHydrateLoad, which is ld(), and ld() RETURNS ITS DEFAULT FOR A STORE THAT WILL NOT PARSE exactly as it does for one that is empty -- so a resource whose local store is unreadable at that instant is seeded EMPTY, the key is written, the done-flag is set, and every row in it is thereafter treated as never-pushed. DRIVEN against the shipped senSyncedBootstrap, senSyncedRead and senServerWinsMerge: with sen_payer_contracts unreadable at bootstrap time the bootstrap returns 'ran' and marks [] for that resource; the store then parses again, the server sends a CORRECTED rate of 145 against a stale local 100, the merge changes NOTHING, and the device keeps 100 permanently. That is the billing-from-memory failure 517c47b1 exists to prevent, arriving through the mechanism added to protect it -- and it lands on precisely the four resources press-on 1 is about, because they are the ones somebody prices work from. IT IS PERMANENT AND SILENT, which is what makes it high rather than moderate: the done-flag is never cleared, so the bootstrap never runs again, and nothing anywhere records that one resource was seeded blind. THE FIX IS THE DISTINCTION THE APP ALREADY MAKES ONE FUNCTION AWAY. senSyncedRead reads the synced map RAW precisely so that absent, unreadable and ok are three answers; the bootstrap reads the DATA through ld(), which collapses two of them. Either read the resource raw and skip marking a resource that could not be read -- leaving it un-seeded so a later bootstrap can do it properly, which needs the done-flag to be per resource rather than per app -- or keep the per-app flag and refuse to set it at all when any resource read came back unreadable. On press-on 2's question as asked, which risk to carry: I would take the partial bootstrap. A bootstrap that has not finished is a state a later load can finish; a resource seeded blind is a wrong answer that is never revisited, and this platform's standing preference is the loud incomplete over the quiet wrong. PRESS-ON 3 IS CLEAN, with a note about how the arm is written rather than about the seams. All three converted auto-push apps really do suppress: the SUPPRESSORS table names sairnfreedom, sairnbiz and stonedesk, the else branch asserts every other app's store seam is a plain st(), and sairnbuild is correctly absent because it is not converted. stonedesk's sdHydrateCustomers write-through is right -- it puts the in-memory sdCustomers through the store before merging so the merge is fed from the store like every other path, and refreshes the global after. THE NOTE: the finally assertion carries `|| A.app === 'stonedesk'`, an exemption BY NAME with no reason beside it. It is safe -- stonedesk's seam delegates to sdWhileSuppressed, which has the finally at stonedesk.html:2283 -- but the arm should assert THAT rather than exempt the app, because an exemption by name is a list that grows and the next app added to it may not have a sdWhileSuppressed. PRESS-ON 4 IS CLEAN, and something landed today is what makes it so. The bootstrap suppressing overwriting for a whole page load cannot strand a device that hydrates only at boot, because the NEXT boot finds the done-flag set and does not suppress. That argument depends entirely on the done-flag actually persisting -- and until 0d0d66c0 today it did not on a full store: the flag write's return was discarded, so every load re-ran the bootstrap and re-suppressed, and server-wins would have been inert on that device forever. The answer to press-on 4 was therefore "yes it can strand" at the moment this obligation was written, and is "no" now. PRESS-ON 5 IS CLEAN. sdHydrateAll returns at `if(!rows||!Array.isArray(rows)||!rows.length)` before anything else, and the SD_SYNCED_OBJECT branch returns on every one of its paths -- adopt only when the key is absent, return on a getItem that throws, return on a non-object blob -- so no object-shaped resource can reach sdServerWinsMerge. The adopt-or-leave rule is untouched and the comment explains why it is not swept in. PRESS-ON 6 IS CLEAN. The one flagged as most at risk is genuinely re-aimed rather than emptied: sairnbiz_server_backup's arm now asserts the local edit survives AND that an unseen server record was appended AND, in the trusted case, that the local row equals the SERVER's value by reference to INV_A.cust rather than to a literal -- three assertions where there was one, and the third is the one that can only pass under the new rule. The never-pushed carve-out is pinned separately by value. VERIFIED ON THE SHIPPED TREE: tests/server_wins_hydration.js 179 arms across all seven apps, tests/run_server_wins_hydration_sabotage_probe.py 21 mutations ALL REFUSED with all seven app files byte-identical, and the sairnsenior, stonedesk, sairnbiz and sairnfreedom suites green. Nothing blocking. The conversion is right, the carve-out is right, and the finding is about a device being admitted to the rule with one resource's worth of the evidence missing.
what:
SERVER-WINS HYDRATION extended to four more apps (sairnsenior, stonedesk, sairnbiz, sairnfreedom) plus a ONE-TIME READ-ONLY BOOTSTRAP added to all seven converted apps. It names sen_claims, sen_pay_rates, sen_payer_contracts and sd_invoices because those Tier A resources are hydrated by the code that changed -- their WRITE paths are untouched.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, hardest first, and the first two are where I am least confident.

(1) sen_payer_contracts, sen_pay_rates, sen_franchise_agreements AND sen_authorizations WERE ALREADY UNCONDITIONAL SERVER-WINS, WITH NO CARVE-OUT, AND I CHANGED THEM. This is the one a reviewer should spend the most time on, because it is a behaviour change to Tier A resources that nobody asked for. sairnsenior shipped ELEVEN hydrates: seven additive-only and these four overwriting any local record whose id the server also held, unconditionally. One file, two opposite conflict rules, neither disclosed. I routed all eleven through one merge, which means these four GAINED the first-push carve-out -- they now KEEP a local record whose own push never landed where before they would have overwritten it. I believe that is strictly better and it is the platform rule. But it is me deciding that a pay rate or a payer contract should be protected in a case where it previously was not, and a reviewer should say whether unifying was right or whether those four were deliberately stricter for a reason I did not find. I looked and found no comment saying so; absence of a comment is not evidence of absence of a reason.

(2) THE BOOTSTRAP'S DONE-FLAG IS PER APP, NOT PER RESOURCE, AND THAT IS A JUDGEMENT. If a device's local store holds nine of eleven sairnsenior resources when the bootstrap runs, the other two are marked seeded as EMPTY and the flag is set. Records for those two arriving later enter through the merge or a landed write and are marked correctly, so I believe nothing is mismarked. The case I cannot rule out is a local store that is temporarily unreadable for ONE resource at bootstrap time -- ld() returns its default, the resource looks empty, and those ids never get seeded, so they are treated as never-pushed and become permanently protected from server corrections. Per-resource flags would avoid it and would also mean a partial bootstrap that never completes. Say which risk is the right one to carry.

(3) THE TWO SEAMS ARE WHERE ALL THE PER-APP RISK LIVES. HydrateLoad and HydrateStore are the only per-app code in the merge path. Four of the seven apps push to the server from inside st(), so a store seam that forgot to suppress would echo every hydrated row straight back to the server -- silently, and only visible under load. Check each of the four (sairnbiz, sairnfreedom, stonedesk, and note sairnbuild is NOT converted) really suppresses, and that stonedesk's sdHydrateCustomers is right: it writes the in-memory sdCustomers global through to the store first, merges, then refreshes the global. That write-through is new and it is the only place the merge is fed from something other than the store.

(4) THE BOOTSTRAP SUPPRESSES OVERWRITING FOR THE WHOLE PAGE LOAD, via a module-level flag rather than per pass. On a load where the bootstrap runs, NOTHING is overwritten anywhere in that app, even by a hydrate that fires much later for an unrelated reason. That is the conservative direction and it is deliberate; check it cannot strand a device that hydrates once at boot and never again.

(5) sd_invoices IS NAMED BECAUSE stonedesk's SD_SYNCED CONTAINS IT. StoneDesk's single-OBJECT resources are deliberately NOT swept into server-wins -- one blob, no ids, nothing to match on, no carve-out to apply -- and their adopt-or-leave rule is untouched. Check that the object branch still runs BEFORE the merge and that no object-shaped resource reaches sdServerWinsMerge().

(6) FOUR PINNED SUITES WERE RE-AIMED, NOT DELETED, and one of them would have KEPT PASSING for the wrong reason: sairnbiz_server_backup's "a locally present id is never overwritten" stays green on a fresh harness because the bootstrap suppresses overwriting on that load. Check the inversions assert the NEW property rather than merely no longer asserting the old one -- an inverted pin that asserts nothing is how a guarantee disappears while the file still looks guarded.

VERIFIED: tests/server_wins_hydration.js 142 arms across all seven apps, including the carve-out over two consecutive merges, both halves of the bootstrap's bounded cost, the corrupt-map path, and a same-rule arm pinning all four helpers identical modulo names. tests/run_server_wins_hydration_sabotage_probe.py 16 mutations ALL REFUSED across seven app files, all restored byte-identical -- including the two the decision specifically asked to be controlled: a bootstrap that skips marking a pre-existing id, and one that marks an id that is not there. checkblocks clean on all seven; every sairnlaw / sairnlegacy / sairndesign / sairnsenior / stonedesk / sairnbiz / sairnfreedom suite green.

You justified 409 with "each of these four READS the row moments before the PATCH". I inventoried all 12 representation-PATCH sites in api/sd-data.js by status code. Six answer 409 (:2219 slab RESERVATION_RACE, :2692, :7577, :7628, :8174, :10466 ALREADY_RESERVED); six answer 404. Your criterion fails: api/sd-data.js:4222 (bld_draws retainage release) reads the draw moments before, and its OWN COMMENT says verbatim "The draw was READ moments ago, so a zero-row match means it moved or went away in between" -- and it answers 404. The criterion that DOES hold for 11 of 12 is different: a SOFT-DELETE answers 404 (:2454, :2628, :10056, :11410, :12652 -- all "nothing was deleted/removed", where the caller asked to remove a thing and the thing is not there, so not-found is the honest answer), and a STATE TRANSITION ON A ROW THAT MUST EXIST answers 409 (issue, pay, set status, promote/decline, reserve -- where the absence contradicts a read the same request just performed and the caller's work is lost). Under that criterion ALL FOUR OF YOURS ARE CORRECT AS WRITTEN. DO NOT UNIFY THEM TO 404. FINDING 1: :4222 is the single outlier -- a money state transition answering the delete-shaped code. It is NOT yours and I have not touched it. Whoever fixes it should write the criterion down next to wroteRow(), because with 12 sites and no stated rule the thirteenth will coin a third answer.

Monotonic, one direction. I grepped sql/ and api/ for every touch of next_seq and of rf_invoice_counters: there is NO decrement, no free-list, no compensating release, and the table carries `check (next_seq >= 1)` with only select/insert/update to service_role and `revoke all from anon, authenticated` -- no delete path either. PostgREST commits the RPC in its own transaction before your PATCH is sent. So a missed PATCH does leave the number spent and attached to nothing. Your sentence is TRUE and should stay.

PRESS-ON 3 (the widened predicate firing on a legitimate branch) -- NO FALSE POSITIVES. I ran your real unguardedIn() against today's api/sd-data.js: it reports []. The two representation-PATCH sites with no wroteRow() call (:2219, :10466) are hand-guarded on rows.length and your `.length === 0` branch clears both correctly. AND A REGRESSION I FOUND IN YOUR SUITE SWEEP THAT IS MINE, NOT YOURS, AND I FIXED IT. You reported "all 29 api/sd-data-*.test.js suites pass".
