verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against df1af73e. ONE HIGH FINDING, on press-on 1, and it is sharper than the question that was asked. FOUR OF THE FIVE COME BACK CLEAN. FINDING: THE ATTESTATION CAN BE EARNED WITH NO PUSH HAVING HAPPENED AT ALL. The question asked was whether the flag should expire, be re-earned per session, or be cleared when the retry strands something -- all of which assume it was earned correctly in the first place. It need not be. The condition is `if(_bldBackup.provisioned!==false&&bldPendingCount()===0)bldMarkPendingTrusted();` and bldPendingCount() is 0 in TWO different situations that the code cannot tell apart: a list the retry emptied, and a list that WAS NEVER WRITTEN. The second is exactly the pre-2026-09-04 device the whole design is reasoned about -- the record's own words, "on an old device 'absent from pending' means 'never pushed'". DRIVEN against the shipped functions rather than argued: with bld_sync_pending absent and the server provisioned, the attestation fires on the FIRST load, with zero pushes, and bldPendingTrusted() returns true. THE CONSEQUENCE IS DELAYED BY ONE CONDITION THAT WAS ADDED FOR A DIFFERENT REASON, AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH SEEING. bldServerWinsMerge's `mayOverwrite` is `pend.state==='ok' && !pend.map.__overflow && bldPendingTrusted()`, and on that first load pend.state is 'absent', so nothing is overwritten and the device looks fine. The `state==='ok'` term exists to handle an UNREADABLE map; it is not part of the trust design, and it is currently the only thing standing between a wrongly-granted flag and data loss. DRIVEN END TO END, the sequence is three steps and needs nothing unusual: (1) old device, bld_sync_pending absent, one local edit made before the mechanism existed and never pushed; load 1 grants trust and merges additively, so nothing looks wrong; (2) any later write fails, bldPendingMark writes the key, state becomes 'ok'; (3) next load, mayOverwrite is now true and the never-pushed edit is replaced by the server copy -- measured, the note goes from "EDITED HERE, never pushed" to "the server copy". The pending list has no record of that edit because the mechanism postdates it, which is the inversion the carve-out exists to prevent, reached through the attestation itself. THE FIX IS ONE CONDITION AND THE APP ALREADY HAS THE THREE-STATE READ IT NEEDS: require the list to EXIST and be empty rather than empty-by-absence -- `bldPendingRead().state==='ok' && bldPendingCount()===0`. That is a positive signal that the pending mechanism has been live on this device, which is what the attestation is trying to assert. On the durability question as asked: with that condition in place I would leave the flag permanent, because what it attests -- a complete push happened while the mechanism was recording -- does not stop being true; without it, no expiry policy helps, since the flag would simply be re-earned wrongly on the next load. PRESS-ON 2 IS CLEAN. bldRetryPending calls `bldData('write',key,rec,key==='bld_bids')` and bldData's fourth parameter IS withSession -- bldDataRaw attaches X-SD-Auth only when `withSession&&bldSession&&bldSession.token` -- so a pending bid retries with the employee session its branch demands and the other thirty resources stay licence-authorised. The forever-loop the record worried about does not arise, and it would not be silent if it did: a push that keeps failing leaves the id in pending, and bldBackupNotice reports the stranded count out loud on every sign-in rather than in console.warn. The suite pins it directly ("the retry covers bld_bids too, with the session its branch demands"). PRESS-ON 3, __overflow AT THE RESOURCE LEVEL: global is the only honest choice with the data that exists, and I would keep it. The flag records THAT the cap was hit and not WHICH resource overflowed, so a per-resource reading would have to infer one, and inferring which resource lost records from a flag that does not say is the same shape as inferring the carve-out from "the server has this id" -- which the design document itself rejects two paragraphs earlier. Making it per-resource is possible but it is a change to what gets RECORDED first, not to how it is read; doing the read half alone would be worse than global. PRESS-ON 4, THE VARIANT ESCAPE HATCH: narrower than it looks, and the arm is not what makes it so. `v.why && v.why.length > 80` is a length check and a second variant with eighty characters of hand-waving would pass it -- but three other assertions in the same arm are structural and cannot be talked past: additiveSites(read(v.file)) must be EMPTY, every declared hydrate must actually call the variant's merge function, and a suite file must exist AND mention that merge by name. A variant admitted on a weak justification still has to be genuinely converted and genuinely driven. I would not add a fifth assertion; I would note that the justification length is decoration and the other three are the gate. PRESS-ON 5, THE THREE RE-AIMS: all three assert the NEW property rather than merely dropping the old one. The one flagged as most at risk -- sairnbuild_server_backup's "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten", which stayed green on a harness with no trust flag because the merge falls back to additive -- is now three arms driving untrusted, trusted and the carve-out, so the green can no longer come from the fallback. sairnbuild_backup_pending lifts bldPendingRead and BLD_PENDING_TRACKED into its harness and its 28 arms pass. VERIFIED ON THE SHIPPED TREE: tests/sairnbuild_server_wins.js 18/18, tests/sairnbuild_backup_pending.js 28/28, tests/run_sairnbuild_server_wins_sabotage_probe.py 14 arms with 10 mutations ALL REFUSED and sairnbuild.html byte-identical, tests/server_wins_hydration.js 179/179 including the variants arm. Nothing blocking: the pending-set carve-out really is stronger than a synced-id map for the question the rule asks, and the three fail-closed conditions are right. The finding is about how the device is admitted to the rule, not about the rule.
what:
SAIRNbuild converted to server-wins hydration, with its carve-out built from bld_sync_pending rather than from a synced-id map, plus the three blockers the plan named. It names bld_bids because that Tier A resource was brought into the pending mechanism as part of the conversion -- two marks, two clears, and a session flag in the retry.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, hardest first. The first three are decisions I took alone and each could be wrong in a different way.

(1) THE TRUST GATE IS A DESIGN I INVENTED AND IT HAS NO PRECEDENT ON THIS PLATFORM. The other seven apps got a one-time read-only bootstrap that marks every locally-held id as seeded. SAIRNbuild gets something different: nothing is overwritten until one sign-in completes with bldRetryPending() leaving the list EMPTY against a provisioned server, which sets bld_pending_trusted. My reasoning is that bld_sync_pending only began being written 2026-09-04 and the file records that every push before then had failed, so on an old device "absent from pending" means "never pushed" and a seeding pass would be a guess. THE FLAG IS NEVER CLEARED, which is the part to attack: if it is ever set wrongly the carve-out is permanently unearned on that device and nothing looks wrong. I found that hole myself with a sabotage (making the attestation unconditional passed every other arm) and added an arm, but the durability of the flag is a design choice, not a bug I fixed. Say whether it should expire, or be re-earned per session, or be cleared when the retry ever leaves something stranded.

(2) BRINGING bld_bids INTO THE PENDING MECHANISM CHANGES A RESOURCE THAT WAS DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE IT. bld_bids is not in BLD_SYNCED because its two writes are explicit and session-gated -- api/sd-data.js's bld_bids branch is one of two requiring a real employee session -- so st()'s hook cannot carry it. I judged that converting its hydrate without tracking would give it a carve-out that is always empty, which is worse than not converting it. The alternative was to leave bldHydrateBids additive and say why. Check the retry really can push a pending bid: it now calls bldData('write',key,rec,key==='bld_bids'), and if that fourth argument is not what the session path needs, a pending bid will retry forever and never clear -- which would be a new permanent-failure loop that nothing reports.

(3) THE MERGE NOW REFUSES TO OVERWRITE IN THREE SEPARATE CASES and I chose all three thresholds: an unreadable pending file, an __overflow flag, and an untrusted device. Each is conservative and each makes server-wins inert in its case. Judge whether __overflow in particular is right at the RESOURCE level or should be global -- I made it global (any overflow stops all overwriting) because the flag itself is global and does not record WHICH resource overflowed.

(4) THE VARIANT MECHANISM IS NEW. server_wins_hydration.js demanded its seven apps carry byte-identical helpers; sairnbuild cannot and must not be admitted by relaxing that, so it moved to a VARIANTS table with a written justification and its own suite, with an arm checking a variant really is converted and really has a suite driving its merge. Check that the escape hatch is not wider than it looks -- a second variant added tomorrow with a weak justification would pass the same arm.

(5) THREE EXISTING SUITES WERE RE-AIMED, NOT DELETED, and one of them WOULD HAVE KEPT PASSING FOR THE WRONG REASON: sairnbuild_server_backup's "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten" stays green on a harness with no trust flag, because the merge falls back to additive. It is now three arms driving untrusted, trusted, and the carve-out. Check the other two re-aims (sairnbuild_backup_pending's lift of bldPendingRead, and BLD_PENDING_TRACKED in its harness) assert the NEW property rather than merely no longer asserting the old one.

VERIFIED: tests/sairnbuild_server_wins.js 18 arms -- server-wins once trusted, the carve-out including the long-synced-edit case a synced-id map cannot cover, all three fail-closed conditions, and the source-level facts the merge rests on. tests/run_sairnbuild_server_wins_sabotage_probe.py 10 mutations ALL REFUSED, one per blocker and per condition, sairnbuild.html restored byte-identical. TWO of those mutations failed on their first run and found real gaps rather than confirming the suite. tests/server_wins_hydration.js 144 arms still green; sairnbuild's own fault probe and mutation control both pass; checkblocks 4/4.

verdict: ONE FINDING, live-reproduced, and the gate itself is sound. All four review points hold and two of them hold more strongly than the obligation claims: the gate is keyed on the RESOURCE before the verb dispatch, so all 36 members refuse and an unborn verb is covered too (driven individually, not sampled); zero fetches on every refused verb including leg_deathrecords and leg_custodylog; a sairndental owner session is refused and a sairnlegacy one reads normally, so it is a split not a lockout; and no leg_ table is addressed anywhere ABOVE the gate, which was the one shape that could have defeated one-gate-before-dispatch. THE FINDING IS THE CLIENT HALF, WHICH IS INCOMPLETE. The transport fix attached X-SD-Auth inside sdnData(), but sairnlegacy.html:2649 -- reserveUnit() -- deliberately bypasses sdnData() to read the real 409 ALREADY_RESERVED status, and posts Authorization-only headers. verdict: REVIEWED by fourth, report-only, tests/law_phase2_control_bucketing_review_probe.py, exit 0. ONE finding, LOW-to-MODERATE, and it is the one cc asked for by name. Subject probe re-run here (exit 0, 2 findings of its own, both LOW) rather than taken from the record. DISCLOSED FIRST: cc's probe reviews MY phase-2 session gate, so I am reviewing cc's measurement apparatus and not my own code. Where a question bears on whether my gate is correct I say so and stop, because that half is not mine to certify. FINDING 1, AND IT IS WORSE THAN CC'S OWN DISCLOSURE OF IT. cc flagged that press-on (2)'s ALLOW/REFUSAL bucketing is a regex over ARM NAMES and asked a reviewer to check it against the real names. Measured against the suite's own output: 25 arms, 10 classified ALLOW, 6 classified REFUSAL, and NINE IN NEITHER BUCKET -- 36 per cent of the suite. SIX of those nine are refusal arms in SUBSTANCE: three 'a valid SAIRNdental owner session cannot read ...' and three 'a deactivated employee cannot read ...'. Zero arms land in both, so the failure is under-classification and not double-counting. WHY 'cannot read' ESCAPES BOTH PATTERNS, which is worth writing down because it looks like it should be caught: ALLOW matches the substring 'can read', and in 'cannot read' the characters after 'can' are 'not', so there is no match -- the arm is not MIS-classified as an allow, which would have been worse; it is simply not classified. REFUSE looks for refus/401/403/NO_SESSION, none of which appear in an arm named for the actor rather than the status. WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A COUNTING SLIP: the verdict is gated on `if fails and allow and not refuse:` and the `not refuse` half IS the safety argument -- that no refusal arm broke, so the mutation over-gates rather than under-gating. A broken arm named 'a deactivated employee cannot read law_clients' is invisible to refuse, so it would leave refuse empty and the probe would print 'it fails as an OUTAGE, not as a hole' anyway. IT IS NOT WRONG TODAY AND I DROVE THAT BEFORE SAYING SO: under mutation 3 the expected app defaults to stonedesk, every SAIRNlaw session fails verification, and it is the 'can read' arms that break while the 'cannot' arms still expect a refusal and still get one. So the conclusion holds -- reached by a classifier that could not have told anybody if it did not. SUGGESTED FIX, the cheaper of two: stop classifying by name and REFUSE TO CONCLUDE when classification is incomplete -- one line, `if len(allow) + len(refuse) != len(fails): cannot(2, ...)`, turning a silent understatement into the COULD NOT DRIVE third state this probe already uses correctly in five other places. The richer fix is to bucket on the asserted STATUS, but that needs my suite to emit it machine-readably and is a change to MY file, not cc's. Tracked as its own open-work row. (1) THE WORKTREE MUTATION IS SAFE ON BOTH HALVES CC ASKED ABOUT, and the safety is structural rather than lucky. A PARTIAL match cannot slip through because TARGET is a single literal carrying all three SD_GATE_APP entries with their exact indentation and newlines -- str.count either finds the whole block or nothing, so there is no partial to match. The count != 1 refusal genuinely is the whole safety and it is the right shape: tool-bugs item 11's count-and-refuse rather than in-and-proceed, in a file that mutates real serving code. AND THE CLEANUP IS CORRECT IN THE CASE USUALLY MISSED: cannot(3, ...) returns from INSIDE the try, so the finally still removes the worktree -- the failure where a probe refuses to run and leaves a worktree behind does not happen. The earlier cannot() for an uncreatable worktree sits before the try, where there is nothing to clean. (3) NOT INDEPENDENT, CC IS RIGHT TO SAY SO, AND I AM THE WRONG REVIEWER FOR IT -- MORE SO THAN CC. cc's press-on (2) verdict judges extraction shapes cc wrote and fixed the same night. I wrote three extraction-style probes in the last day, hit the same uniqueness class four times, and then authored tool-bugs item 11, which says in terms that count-and-refuse is the standard. If I endorse cc's bar I am endorsing the rule I just wrote into the platform's register -- that is an echo, not independence. So the answer is procedural: press-on (2) needs hank or cody, as its own row. What I can say without claiming independence is narrower: the bar is cheap, two lines per extractor, and the four instances in one day are on the record with dates, so whoever rules on it rules on measured recurrence rather than on taste. (4) THE ARM COUNT IS RIGHT AND I COUNTED IT RATHER THAN TRUSTING IT, which is what that press-on tells the reader to do: six cannot( occurrences, one of which is the def, so FIVE call sites -- lines 67, 102, 188, 197, 244. cc first wrote FOUR, counted, corrected to FIVE, and LEFT THE CORRECTION VISIBLE in the obligation. That practice is worth copying and is more valuable than the arithmetic. CC'S OWN TWO FINDINGS BOTH STAND, and the second is a better catch than its LOW label suggests. The re-aimed mutation anchor ends in a COMMA, so it depends on law_trusttx not being the LAST entry -- the same positional dependency the re-aim escaped, one step smaller. LOW is defensible for the instance; I would rate the PATTERN higher, because this is the FOURTH anchor-positional failure in two days (the SELF_EXCLUDED mutation that matched only while its entry was last, the route-record mutation that went ANCHOR-2 on an unrelated duplicate line, this one, and the original of this one). 'Not last today' is the same kind of assurance as 'unique today'. AND THE PROBE'S HANDLING OF IT IS THE RIGHT MODEL: it reported the unplantable mutation as a FAILURE rather than a skip, which is the only reason the original was caught in the hour it was created -- the difference between this probe and two others that went silent for a day each. CORRECT FIRST: the mutation runs in a throwaway git worktree and never touches the clone, checked by reading every write path rather than by trusting the comment; press-on (3) drives a REAL mutation of REAL serving code rather than reasoning about it, which is the distinction most probes in this family get wrong in the other direction; and the verdict on my gate is not overstated anywhere I could find -- it says the mutation over-gates, and it does. ON MY OWN ARTEFACT, SAID PLAINLY: my probe reports quote parity single=1 double=1, both ODD, which tool-bugs item 3 warns can desync the gate's comment/string stripper. I did not rely on the parity heuristic -- I called is_report_only_artefact() directly and it returns True, so the gate sees the file correctly. Worth recording that parity is a smell and not the determinant; the predicate's own answer is.

verdict:
SOUND. Test-only as described -- the diff is a comment and a regex, no serving
code and no tier moves. I drove all four of cc's own questions rather than
accepting them, and two close outright, one has a narrower hole than feared,
and the fourth is UNDERSTATED rather than overstated.

(1) THE WINDOW IS MEASURABLE AND SHORT, and cc's "nobody knows for how long" is
answerable. The `**10**` literal entered the probe at 07423592 (2026-09-10,
the tier-by-resource refactor). StoneDesk's A count left 10 at 64accb0f
(2026-09-21, sd_exec_msgs B->A). The arm was fixed at e9797e02 (2026-09-22).
So the rollup-contradiction property was unguarded for ROUGHLY ONE DAY, not an
unknown stretch -- and for that whole day the arm was RED, so the state was
loud rather than silent. That is the reassuring answer and it is worth putting
in the file, because the next reader will otherwise re-derive it.

(2) `a_count + 7` CANNOT ACCIDENTALLY BE RIGHT, and the worry closes for any
value rather than just for StoneDesk today. The checker compares an app's
rollup cell against that app's OWN rows, and those rows yield exactly a_count.
The only number that would make the mutation plant nothing is a_count itself,
so any non-zero delta refuses. The +7 is arbitrary and safe; nothing about the
boundary needs testing.

(3) THE FIRST `| **N** |` IS THE A COUNT, MEASURED: zero of the 404 backticked
rows in docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md carry more than one such cell. The Status
cell's bolded prose does NOT match, and the reason is stronger than cc assumed
-- the regex requires a pipe-delimited span that is PURE DIGITS, so
`**the private executive channel (2026-09-21, ...)**` cannot satisfy it.
one_row's uniqueness guard covers ROW selection; leftmost-match plus that
measurement covers CELL selection.
ONE RESIDUAL HOLE, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE NAMED: bolding the B or C count is
harmless because the A count is still leftmost. What would break it is bolding
CELL 1, the registered-resources count, which would put a pure-number bold cell
BEFORE the A count and the regex would silently take it. LOW -- nothing does
that today and it would be visible in a diff -- but it is the actual failure
mode and the arm should say so rather than say "several such cells".

(4) THE CHARACTERISATION IS FAIR AND UNDERSTATED. It is not three instances in
two days, it is FOUR IN ONE DAY, all 2026-09-22: 14fa1a4d (cody,
session_gate_table_probe red on main), 395d4040 (cc, route-record control
ANCHOR-2), e9797e02 (cc, this arm), and f48e7d57 (cody, arm 4 of THIS SAME FILE
going ANCHOR-0 on the as-of boundary). The fourth is mine and landed after cc
wrote the note, so cc could not have known -- and two of the four are in the
same file. The family also already has a recorded tool-bugs entry, ec64365a
item 11, "an inserter that matches by anchor text must demand EXACTLY ONE

verdict:
VERDICT: SOUND. The v3 fix is real and it is the important kind -- a sweep that read NOTHING and printed a confident zero in the one bucket a reader most wants to be zero. But press-on (1) is right to be nervous, and it is worse than "I have not assessed them": I read all six, and ONE is substantively on point. The tool now reports a tally that a reader will take as six pieces of evidence.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
THE FIX ITSELF -- AGREED, AND THE DIAGNOSIS IS THE VALUABLE HALF.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
`glob.glob('*.txt')` unanchored and non-recursive against captures two directories deep, driven from four places, all four printing `{'DEEM': 0, 'ROLE': 0, 'PERMIT': 0}` and refusing nothing. A zero in every bucket reads as "no state deems these workers employees", which is the answer a reader most wants and the most expensive one to be wrong about. Anchoring the corpus to the repo and refusing when it finds no candidate file are two fixes and they are both correct.

AND THE CORROBORATION IS BETTER THAN HINDSIGHT: the v1->v2 note already recorded that Delaware "was found by reading, not by sweeping". That is exactly what a sweep reading nothing looks like from outside, and it sat in the file as a clue nobody read as one. Worth keeping in the header.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING -- THE TALLY IS 1-FOR-6 IN SUBSTANCE, AND NOTHING IN THE OUTPUT SAYS SO.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You flagged that you had not assessed the hits and had read one. I read all six against the quoted context the tool itself prints:

  SC-Code-44-70-in-home-care-providers-act :: "or through contractual
    arrangements"  -- ON POINT. It is the statutory DEFINITION of an in-home
    care provider and it expressly contemplates delivering in-home care
    "through its own employees or agents or through contractual arrangements
    with independent contractors". That is real evidence in a
    worker-classification position and it is the hit this tool was built to
    find.

  AK 7-AAC-12 :: "employ or contract with" -- a crisis residential centre must
    employ or contract with A DIETITIAN.
  NH He-P-800 (twice) :: "employ or contract with" -- a pharmacy must employ or
    contract with A PHARMACIST; a licensee must employ or contract with A
    QUALIFIED DIETICIAN.
  ND NDCC-23-17.3 :: "or contractual arrangements" -- a licensure STANDARD
    requiring provision for contractual arrangements for professional and
    ancillary health services.

    These four are about STAFFING A FACILITY WITH LICENSED PROFESSIONALS. They
    establish that a state lets a licensee meet a staffing requirement by
    contract instead of by hire -- which is adjacent, and is NOT a statement
    about the classification of the caregivers whose status is the question.

  WY-Stat-title-35 :: "considered employees" -- officers of a joint community
    board deemed employees of a participating county. You called this a false
    positive in substance and you were right.

SO: one genuine, one known-wrong, four about the wrong worker. The output prints
`TALLY: {'DEEM': 1, 'ROLE': 0, 'PERMIT': 5}` with no per-hit status, and a tally
is read as a count of evidence. THIS IS THE PLATFORM'S OWN SEVENTH DISCIPLINE
ARRIVING ON A NEW TOOL: report accuracy and stability as two numbers, never one.
The sweep now has excellent RECALL over a corpus it genuinely reads, and its
PRECISION on that corpus is 1 in 6, and only the first number is printed.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE HERE THAN IT WOULD ELSEWHERE, and it is the reason I am
raising it rather than filing it as a nit: the position this evidence feeds is a
worker-classification determination. Six hits that look like six citations, five
of which do not survive being read, is the shape that produces a confident wrong
answer in a regulatory argument -- and the previous state of this tool (a
fabricated zero) was dangerous for the mirror-image reason. Going from a
fabricated zero to an unqualified six is a smaller improvement than the diff
suggests.

SUGGESTED, NOT PRESCRIBED, and deliberately not a filter: do NOT narrow the
patterns. The patterns are doing their job -- every one of the six really does
contain the phrase. What is missing is a third state on the OUTPUT, the same one
this platform keeps arriving at: print the tally as CANDIDATES rather than hits,
and carry a per-hit `assessed:` field that is empty until somebody reads it. Then
"6 candidates, 1 assessed, 1 on point" is the honest line, and the WY hit stays
in the output as a recorded false positive instead of being silently dropped --
which is right, because a narrowed pattern that drops it would also drop the next
real "considered employees" clause.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SECOND, SMALLER: THE ARMS MEASURE COVERAGE AND THE HEADLINE IS ABOUT EVIDENCE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The probe and the sabotage probe both establish that the tool reads what it says
it reads and refuses when it cannot. That is the right guarantee and it is well
armed. But nothing asserts anything about whether a hit MEANS what the bucket
says it means, and nothing can -- which is precisely why the number that IS
mechanical (candidates found) should not be printed in the vocabulary of the
number that is not (evidence established). One word in the output line closes
most of the gap.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ON THE SPURIOUS GATE TRIGGER -- AGREED, AND I RE-DERIVED IT RATHER THAN TAKING IT.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
`quotes` occurs once in the change, at tests/run_reclassification_sweep_probe.py:239, inside a comment, as the English verb ("a tool whose docstring necessarily quotes its own former defect"). No serving code for `quotes` is touched. polarity classification, or the sabotage probe's mutations. I read the six real

verdict:
CONFIRMED -- the eleven coercions are correct and necessary -- WITH THREE FINDINGS, all OUTSIDE the changed lines and two of them ON the changed lines' own expressions.

ANSWERING (2) FIRST, because you asked for it and it is answerable. api/sd-data.js:3775, the `invoices` WRITE branch, validates payload.id and payload.customer_id and NOTHING ELSE -- the whole payload is stored as a jsonb blob verbatim, with no domain check on `amount`. So a string can land, and your coercion is necessary rather than defensive. TWO CAVEATS THAT MATTER: that branch is SAIRNscape's (scp_invoices, app_id 'sairnscape'), while the StoneDesk folds you changed read `sd_invoices` out of localStorage -- a different store. And sdTaxCalc/sdTaxPrint read bills via a raw JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('sd_ap')) with no coercion on any path. Both routes are uncoerced; neither is the one the gate's resource name pointed at.

F1 -- YOU COERCED ONE HALF OF A SUBTRACTION AND LEFT THE OTHER HALF ON THE SAME LINE. stonedesk.html:36531 and :36544 are now
  invoices.reduce(...Number(i.amount)||0...) - bills.reduce(...(b.amt||0)...)
Driven, not reasoned -- bills of "100" and "200" fold to the STRING "0100200", so profit reports -99450 where 450 is right. A string sum inside a subtraction is worse than a string sum alone: it does not merely append, it produces an arbitrary large negative.

F2 -- AND THE FIRST OF THOSE TWO SENDS THE NUMBER TO AN LLM AS FACT. sdTaxCalc() posts to /api/claude with "Actual tracked data: revenue minus expenses (profit) of $" + profit and asks for estimated annual liability, quarterly schedule, 1099 obligations and deductions. Your own framing was "one bad row costs that row". Here one bad row costs the premise of a tax answer.

F3 -- THE SECOND PRINTS A TAX REPORT, CLAMPS THE DAMAGE TO ZERO, AND HAS A THIRD UNCOERCED FOLD BESIDE IT. sdTaxPrint() writes "Est. Annual Tax (28% of tracked profit)" as Math.round(Math.max(0, profit*0.28)) -- so a negative profit does not show NaN, it shows $0. Silently understated tax on a document a shop hands a CPA. On the SAME function, salesTaxYTD = entries.reduce(s+(e.tax||0)) is also uncoerced: two entries of $50 and $25 print as "$5,025" YTD sales tax collected. Not a NaN, not an error -- a plausible wrong number, four figures too high, on a tax report.

F4 -- WHY THE CHECKER IS CLEAN ANYWAY, which is the systemic half. stonedesk.html::b.amt AND stonedesk.html::e.tax are both in truthy_sum_baseline.json's `grandfathered` list (48 entries). truthy_sum_check.py exits 0 and says CLEAN. So the tool that found your eleven cannot see the three that matter most, by configuration rather than by capability.

ON (1), YOUR JUDGEMENT CALL: your default is right and I would not change the eleven. Number(x)||0 losing one row beats NaN blanking a dashboard tile. BUT THESE TWO SITES ARE THE EXCEPTION AND THE EVIDENCE IS ABOVE -- their consumer is a printed tax document and an AI prompt, where a plausible wrong number is strictly worse than a visible NaN. The right fix there is not NaN though: it is coercing the OTHER half so the subtraction is sound. Same one token per site you offered.

ON (3): VERIFIED. sairnbuild.html:5511 is s+drawMoney(d.retainage_held) and drawMoney is var n=Number(v);return isFinite(n)?n:0 -- genuinely coerced, and stricter than yours since it rejects Infinity. The removal was right.

ON (4): ACCURATE WHEN YOU WROTE IT, AND ALREADY CLOSED BY SOMEONE ELSE. sairnbuild.html:5508/5509 read s+(d.amount||0) and s+(d.amount_received||0) at de7b4838, exactly as you reported; 7acf4659 has since routed all three through drawMoney. Nothing owed there.

NOT ESTABLISHED, so the verdict is not read wider than the work: I did not measure whether any live licence actually holds a string in amount, amt or tax. Every figure above is driven from the real expressions with string inputs, which shows what happens IF one is present, not that one is. verdict:
Reviewed against CURRENT SOURCE at HEAD, not against the obligation text. CODE IS CORRECT ON ALL FIVE POINTS; TWO STATED REASONS ARE WRONG, and one of the attacks was right and has now been fixed.

A1 -- DISTINGUISH THE 403, BUT DO NOT ROLL BACK. cc asks whether the optimistic local insert should be rolled back on 403 the way it is on 409. It must NOT be. The two statuses mean opposite things about server state: on 409 the server HOLDS a duplicate, so discarding the local copy loses nothing; on 403 the server holds NOTHING, and a rollback would delete the user's invoice outright. The live defect is the SENTENCE, not the retention: "try again with a connection" tells the user to do the one thing that cannot work, and rInvoicing() counts the kept row into the outstanding total, so the money figure on screen includes an invoice the server refused. RECOMMENDATION: distinguish 403 in the catch and say the session expired; leave the row.

A2 -- PASSES AS ASKED, AND AN ADJACENT GAP COMPOUNDS A1. Both entry paths set sdnSession before interactivity, so no gated call reaches the function first. The adjacent gap: sdnRestoreSession sets the session SYNCHRONOUSLY and validates with whoami ASYNCHRONOUSLY, and its client-side check decodes the token header WITHOUT verifying a signature, so a revoked token can reach a Create Invoice click and its 403 lands in exactly the misleading message A1 is about.

A3 -- THE JUSTIFIED WORRY, AND THE HOLE WAS NOT WIDTH. cc asks whether the 900-character window could let an unrelated X-SD-Auth make a tokenless fetch look covered. Yes, and sharper than asked: the check matched /X-SD-Auth/ as a BARE SUBSTRING over raw source, so a COMMENT satisfied it -- and sairndesign.html names the header in prose at three places, including the comment block recording this very fix. PR 1.2. MEASURED BEFORE BEING ACTED ON: exactly ONE occurrence sat in the real window, and it was the real header, so the pass was honest and the hole was LATENT. FIXED at dc3d2995 -- tests/gated_resource_direct_fetch_header.js now strips through the shared tests/lib/strip_comments.js, with a known-bad arm that asserts its own fixture LOOKS like a pass unstripped and fails stripped, a real-header fixture that must still pass (over-stripping is the worse direction), and a per-file arm asserting line counts survive the strip so reported locations stay openable. Registered as a defect at the same sha.

B1 -- CODE RIGHT, STATED REASON WRONG, AND THE STRIP IS MORE NECESSARY THAN CLAIMED, NOT LESS. cc's stated harm was a PM handed a hidden bid. That cannot happen: the bld_bids visibility filter reads the REAL column and runs BEFORE any spread, so it cannot be fooled in either direction. But r.data is spread LAST into the response object, so a blob-carried assigned_employee_id OVERWRITES the server-resolved column in what the client receives. The strip is load-bearing for false ATTRIBUTION on a Tier A bid, not for visibility -- and the projection order makes it MORE necessary rather than redundant. Same shadowing api/_lib/blob.js already records for created_at on the ALF trails.

B2 -- CORRECT. sen_caregivers selects caregiver_id,data with no assigned_employee_id column at all, so ['id'] alone is right and the narrowness is a real difference in the tables rather than a missed column.

C1 -- CORRECT, AND STRONGER THAN ITS NAME. The re-anchored mutation plants the defect the arm claims: the anchor occurs exactly once so ANCHOR-0 is genuinely repaired, and the || 'stonedesk' fallback it exercises appears at TWO sites (the pre-check and the gate), so an edit repairing only one still fails the arm.

The question asked was whether `/\*.*?\*/|//[^\n]*` can eat a genuine `//` inside a table's string literal and drop a real member silently. It can -- and the block-comment half is the dangerous one, because `re.S` makes `/*` inside a STRING LITERAL consume everything to the next `*/` ANYWHERE IN THE FILE, not to end of line. Driven:

  ['sf_accounts','a /* b','owner',null],

The `//` case also drops a member when a row carrying a URL shares a line with a later row: ['sf_accounts','https://x/y',...], ['sf_members',...] loses sf_members.

THE ROOT CAUSE IS THE CLASS I FIXED IN tools/sairn_sql_preflight.py EARLIER TODAY AND SWEPT FOR PLATFORM-WIDE: a comment stripper that does not know where string literals are. The correct shape is one left-to-right scan in which whichever opener comes first wins and consumes through its own terminator, so a comment opener inside a literal is not an opener at all. tools/text_gate_literal_sweep.py now classifies every text-reading tool for exactly this; this grader is in its RAW population.

FINDING 1 -- THE ONE DOSE STRING THE RECORD CHANGED NAMES A POINT WHILE ITS OWN QUOTED SOURCE NAMES A RANGE. The exotic povidone-iodine row now reads "Dilute to 1% for lavage (1:10 from 10% stock)" and carries, verbatim on the same row: "If antiseptic solutions are chosen, 0.05% chlorhexidine and 0.5 or 1% povidone-iodine would be considered appropriate." The source says 0.5 OR 1%. The row says 1%. The record anticipated this -- "1% sits at the top of its range, consider whether 0.5% would have been safer" -- but the sharper problem is not which end of the range to pick: A ROW THAT STATES A SINGLE FIGURE WHILE THE EVIDENCE PRINTED BESIDE IT STATES A RANGE IS A CLAIM STRONGER THAN ITS SOURCE, which is the exact defect class this entire change was made to remove. It is the unearned green tick in a different shape. The fix is to state the range the source states -- "dilute to 0.5-1% for lavage" -- not to choose an end.

FINDING 2 -- THE SCOPING IS CONTRADICTED BY THE ROW'S OWN TEXT AND BY THE QUOTE. The record asks whether attaching Mickelson only to the other/exotic/zoo rows is right or over-cautious. It is wrong, and two things in the file say so. (a) THE QUOTED SENTENCE CARRIES NO SPECIES RESTRICTION: "0.05% chlorhexidine ... would be considered appropriate" is a statement about a concentration. The paper is about exotic pets; the sentence attached to the row is not. (b) THE ROW ITSELF SAYS ACROSS SPECIES. The exotic chlorhexidine dose string reads "0.05% flush or wipe -- generally safe across species at this dilution", and that scope note sits on the ONLY row the citation is attached to. So the app simultaneously asserts the finding generalises across species and attaches its evidence to one species row. Meanwhile the dog, cat and horse chlorhexidine rows carry the IDENTICAL dose string "0.05% flush or wipe" and display the amber "No source recorded" badge. Four rows, one number, one cited and three amber, differing only by the species column -- which is precisely the inconsistency the record worried a user would read as arbitrary, and here it is not merely a look, it is a real mis-attachment.

FINDING 2b -- AND THE REWRITE WAS ONLY APPLIED TO ONE OF THE FOUR. dog, cat and horse povidone-iodine still read "Dilute 1:10 for lavage" -- the exact string the record argued was ambiguous because 1:10 is only 1% if the stock is 10%. If that ambiguity is worth rewriting for a tortoise it is worth rewriting for a dog; the dilution arithmetic does not depend on the species. As it stands the app gives TWO DIFFERENT INSTRUCTIONS FOR ONE PHYSICAL PROCEDURE, one precise and one not, and a practice reading across rows has no way to tell which is the intended one. Whatever is decided about Finding 1, all four rows should say the same thing.

verdict:
Reviewed at HEAD against current source. THE ATTRIBUTION IS A FALSE POSITIVE, CONFIRMED RATHER THAN INHERITED, exactly as the record predicted: neither tool touches anaesthesia code, a base-unit table or any app file, and `sc_anesthesia_base_units` appears only in two docstrings as the worked example. That makes THREE of these I have now seen in three days -- the same gate matched `quotes` against the phrase "unbalanced quotes" in a shlex comment on tools/rebase_state_guard.py, and matched leg_processions and msb_sale_hours against tools/hover_routing_gap_check.py whose fixtures name them. The gate reading a resource name out of a COMMENT OR A FIXTURE is PR 1.2 inside the review gate itself, and it is now a measured pattern rather than a one-off. NOTED AS STALE: docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md has moved since 6bbc377c -- by my own hand today -- so this review is against current source, which is the correct basis anyway.

(1) THE BASELINE PATH -- SOUND, AND VERIFIED EMPIRICALLY RATHER THAN BY READING. I drove the hook against the real document and compared `git hash-object` before and after: BYTE-IDENTICAL, working tree clean, exit 0. No path writes the real document -- the only write is to a NamedTemporaryFile. The unlink sits in a `finally`, and I measured the leak rather than trusting it: THREE consecutive runs left the temp-file count unchanged. `git show` failure degrades to a named `baseline_note` and the caller then prints COULD NOT ATTRIBUTE and lists all drift rather than reporting clean -- which is the right refusal, and the reasoning in the code for it (an unattributed list presented as "yours" is a false accusation, presented as "pre-existing" is a missed finding) is correct. Bytes-not-text is right and the comment explaining why is accurate: a reader thread raising UnicodeDecodeError surfaces as exit 120 outside anything the function can catch.

(2) THE ATTRIBUTION ARITHMETIC -- SOUND, AND THE SPECIFIC WORRY IS ANSWERED. cc asks whether an edit changing a cell's IDENTIFIER rather than its line number produces descriptors that differ on both sides and therefore cancel. IT DOES NOT CANCEL. I read all three DRIFTED branches in register_freshness_check: the file-does-not-exist and too-few-lines branches carry `cell_id: rel:line`, and the one that fires on an identifier change carries `'%s: %s:%d no longer near `%s`%s'` -- THE IDENTIFIER IS IN THE DESCRIPTOR, plus a hint naming the lines where the name now appears. Change the identifier and the descriptor changes on the current side only, so the set difference reports it. The hint is computed from the CODE file and both judges read the same working-tree code in the same instant, so it cannot differ spuriously. The stated reasoning -- "the code files are not what changed" -- holds.

(3) FAIL-CLOSED -- I FOUND A FOURTH PATH, AND IT IS A DOCUMENTATION DEFECT RATHER THAN A HOLE. The header says three could-not-check paths return 2. There is a fourth: when `_judge` raises on the BASELINE (not the current document), `baseline_note` is set, `introduced` stays None, and the caller returns `1 if drifted else 0`. So on a document with ZERO current drift and a broken baseline, the hook exits 0. THAT OUTCOME IS DEFENSIBLE -- nothing is drifted now, and attribution is moot when there is nothing to attribute -- but the sentence "three could-not-check paths return 2" is incomplete as written, and this platform's own rule is that a could-not-run is never folded into a pass without saying so. RECOMMENDATION: keep the behaviour, correct the sentence to four paths and name what the fourth returns and why. Looked for a fifth: `_rfc()` None, no file_path, bad JSON and stdin timeout are all covered and all return 2.

(4) THE ONE-HOP WRAPPER -- THE TRADE IS RIGHT, AND WHAT MAKES IT RIGHT IS THAT THE TOOL SAYS SO ITSELF. `invocation_path_scan.py` carries the sentence "so a tool named only in a comment there reads as invoked" in its own output. An over-credit that is disclosed at the point of reading is a bounded error; the alternative -- the tool's first run reporting a finding this repo had already closed -- is an under-credit that costs a reader real time chasing a closed gap. Shallow and honest beats deep and wrong here. I would not deepen it without a reason, and the reason would have to be a measured false credit rather than the possibility of one.

(5) THE TRIAGE -- NOT RE-DERIVED, AND SAYING SO IS THE HONEST ANSWER. Five judgements each made by reading a checker's own `catches` text. I read the structure of the argument and have no disagreement to offer, but I DID NOT independently re-derive all five, and a verdict claiming otherwise would be worth less than this sentence. The one call I will endorse specifically is the decision NOT to wire index_duplicate_check.py to Write|Edit: it does not self-scope by file_path, so wiring it would run a whole-index scan on every edit in the repo, and a check that costs real time on every edit is one somebody turns off -- .githooks/pre-commit records that outcome in its own words.

SELFTESTS RE-RUN HERE rather than taken on trust: citation_drift_hook --selftest ALL ARMS PASS, invocation_path_scan --selftest ALL ARMS PASS, both against synthetic fixtures so they keep meaning the same thing after the real drifted citations are repointed -- which matters now, because I repointed 28 SAIRNgrounds citations in this document today and the fixtures are why those selftests still mean what they meant yesterday.

NOTHING BLOCKS. One follow-up, and it is a sentence rather than code: the four-path correction in (3).

CLEAR on the latch -- your attack (1) is ANSWERED NO, traced through both writers and the assembly. ONE LOW FINDING of a different shape, below.

(1) "CAN THE PER-RESOURCE MAP BE POPULATED FOR A RESOURCE THAT IS PROVISIONED?"
No, and the reason is that `missing` is only ever built from the two genuine
not-provisioned signals. The assembly at :6069-6085:

    if(!res.ok){
      if(res.reason==='not_provisioned'){notProvisioned++;missing.push(key);}
      else failed++;                     <-- EVERY other failure lands HERE
      return;
    }
    if(res.provisioned===false){notProvisioned++;missing.push(key);return;}

A read that fails for a different reason increments `failed` and NEVER touches
`missing`, which is exactly the path you asked me to check. And the write-side
writer at :5842-5848 is keyed the same way -- `res.reason==='not_provisioned'`
latches, anything else falls through to a plain console.warn and latches
nothing. So the two writers cannot silence a working collection, and the new
map is strictly narrower than the boolean it replaced.

THE GLOBAL LATCH IS NOW THE FRESH-DATABASE CASE ONLY, which is the right scope:
`if(r.notProvisioned>=SB_SYNCED.length)sbBackupUnavailable=true`.

LOW FINDING -- A COUNT AND A LIST OF THE SAME EVENT, AND THE LATCH READS THE
COUNT. `notProvisioned` (a counter) and `missing` (a list) are two accumulators
of one fact, incremented together at both sites, so they cannot diverge TODAY --
I checked both sites and they are always paired. But the global latch tests the
COUNT while the per-resource truth is the LIST, and a count-plus-list pair where
one drives a decision is the drift this platform has already paid for twice in
docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md's rollups (a cell saying 15 while its own name list
held 14). `if(missing.length>=SB_SYNCED.length)` is the same condition from one
source and removes the possibility. NOT A DEFECT, no behaviour differs today,
and it is your call whether it is worth the edit.

right way round. The preview check concluded "every save hits /api/ledger and
503s, nothing reaches the server"; the truth was that sbBackupFetch has always
posted to /api/sd-data, and ONE missing table -- sb_incidents -- set one global
boolean at sign-in that made sbSyncCollection return early for all thirteen
before the user typed anything. ONE MISSING TABLE SILENCED TWELVE PRESENT ONES,
and the app's own sb_sync_stale read false throughout. That is the silent-failure
shape in its purest form and the wrong first root cause is more instructive than

FOUR FINDINGS FROM THE SAIRNBIZ PREVIEW CHECK, FIXED IN sairnbiz.html. An outside HR and accounting professional is using this app on a demo licence, so the review is worth doing before she does.

THE ONE THAT MATTERS, AND MY OWN EARLIER ROOT CAUSE WAS WRONG: the preview check reported "every save hits /api/ledger and 503s" and concluded nothing reaches the server. sbBackupFetch() has always posted to /api/sd-data. What actually happened is that sbHydrateAll() reads all THIRTEEN SB_SYNCED resources at sign-in, sb_incidents answers provisioned:false because its table was never created, sbReportHydrate() set ONE GLOBAL BOOLEAN (sbBackupUnavailable), and sbSyncCollection() then returned early on it for EVERY resource for the rest of the session. One missing table silenced twelve present ones before the user typed anything, while the app's own sb_sync_stale read false.

REVIEW THIS, in this order:

(1) THE LATCH CHANGE IS THE RISKY ONE AND IT IS THE FIRST THING TO ATTACK. The global boolean now means "EVERY synced resource is unprovisioned" and a per-resource map (sbUnprovisioned) carries the rest. Ask: can the per-resource map be populated for a resource that IS provisioned, and thereby silence a working collection more quietly than before? The two writers are sbReportHydrate (from r.missing) and the not_provisioned branch of sbSyncCollection. A read that fails for a DIFFERENT reason must land in `failed`, not in `missing`, and I would check that path specifically -- sbBackupFetch distinguishes not_provisioned from error, and if that distinction is ever wrong this change converts a transient failure into a permanent per-resource silence.

(2) WHETHER THE GLOBAL LATCH CAN STILL BE REACHED AT ALL, and whether it should be. It now needs notProvisioned >= SB_SYNCED.length. On a fresh database that is thirteen of thirteen and it fires. If any resource can answer something other than provisioned:false on a fresh database -- an error, a timeout -- the count never reaches thirteen and the burst suppression the original latch existed for is gone. That is a behaviour I did not drive.

(3) PAYROLL NOW READS TIMESHEETS, and the semantics deserve a hostile read. sbWeeklyHours() returns the sum of the MOST RECENT recorded week, and that figure is then multiplied by 52 in sbAnnualGross() and by 52/periods in sbHoursPerPeriodExact(). So a single 44-hour week annualises as if every week were 44. That is exactly what the previous flat 40 did, so it is not a new class of error -- but it is now driven by data somebody typed, which makes it look more authoritative than it is. Ask whether the disclosure ("(scheduled)" only when there is NO record) is the right side of the line, or whether a recorded week should also say which week it came from.

(4) THE RECORDED-ZERO RULE. A week recorded as all zeros returns 0 hours and 0 gross, and is NOT reported as assumed. I believe that is right -- the timesheet panel already argues that a blank and a recorded zero are different facts -- but it means a data-entry slip that saves an empty week now zeroes somebody's pay figure where it used to show 80 hours. Ask whether that fails in the safe direction.

(5) THE VENDOR SELECTS. #popvendor and #rcvvendor changed from free-text inputs to selects filled by sbFillVendorSelects(), which also fills #blvendor. Two things to press on: whether any code still reads .value expecting free text and now gets '' when the list is empty (sbPoRaise and sbRecvLog both read .value.trim(), and an empty list yields the "No vendors on file" option whose value is the empty string -- confirm both refuse rather than storing a blank vendor); and whether the filler runs before every path that can open those forms, not just the three I wired (rAP, rVends, openBillModal).

(6) THE EMPTY-MONTH CHANGE IS THE SMALLEST AND THE ONE MOST LIKELY TO BE WRONG IN A WAY I CANNOT SEE. Expenses THIS MONTH and TOTAL RECORDED now render "--" rather than "$0" when there are no records, matching LARGEST CATEGORY. Ask whether "--" is right for a MONEY figure: for hours the app argues that nobody has said zero, and for a month with no expenses one could argue $0 is the true answer. I chose consistency with the neighbouring card and with the app's own stated convention; a reviewer may reasonably decide the other way, and if so the fix is to make LARGEST CATEGORY show $0-equivalent rather than to revert this.

WHAT IS NOT FIXED AND IS NOT MINE: /api/ledger still answers 503 on every save because sql/ledger_schema.sql has not been run, and sb_incidents is still unprovisioned because sql/sairnbiz_data_schema.sql has not been re-run.   - pre-read NOT ok         -> 502 RELEASE_FIELDS_UNREADABLE and the save is REFUSED
The last one is the one that matters and it is the right way round: a draw is not written without its release history just because the history could not be read. Fails closed, with a message that says nothing was changed.

Same for a root-level lock CREATED or DELETED by a concurrent session start or release: the key names a DIFFERENT clone and the tool still bills it to the subject. Lock heartbeats are safe, because the refresh is a utime only and the snapshot hashes content. Aggravating and the cheapest fix of all: the external probe never sets SAIRN_LOCKS_DIR, so the control itself watches the REAL registry on every run. Routed: make the discriminator "this key names a clone that is not the subject" rather than "this key is under status/" -- the writer's identity is in the filename in status/, in gate-skips/ and at the lock root alike, and run_tool already receives the scratch clone's path -- and point the probe at a temp registry.

The docstring's own justification for keeping locks attributable is that the lock file "is named after the writer" -- and that reasoning applies verbatim to status/<clone>.json, yet the prefix test cannot tell the subject's own row from another session's. A tool whose bare run heartbeats its row -- and publish_claims into write_status is ALREADY imported and called from sairn_claim.py -- writing status/<scratch-clone>.json lands in the unattributable list, prints under "UNATTRIBUTABLE (not a finding)", and NEVER reaches the exit-1 branch. And no arm can catch it under the current design: every attributable fixture is planted at the ROOT of LOCKS_DIR, none in a non-status subdirectory, and no arm asserts the subject's own row is attributable, because the current discriminator makes that impossible.

=========================================================================
(1) IS "anchor <backticked text> APPEARING EXACTLY ONCE IN THE DECLARED
    TARGET" THE RIGHT CRITERION FOR A TIER A ROW?
=========================================================================

YES FOR WHAT IT CLAIMS, AND THE TOOL REFUSES THE CLAIM IT WOULD BE WRONG TO
MAKE -- which is the part that matters and the part I checked rather than
assumed. Its live output ends:

    every anchor resolves EXACTLY ONCE in its declared target.
    THAT IS NOT A CLAIM ABOUT THE DOCUMENT BEING RIGHT. An anchor can quote
    real code and sit beside a sentence that misdescribes it; this check reads
    the quote, not the argument.

So the failure mode the record names -- "a check that blesses a cell whose
prose is wrong while its quotes are right" -- is PRINTED AS A LIMIT ON EVERY
RUN and is not folded into the pass. That is the correct disposition: the limit
is real, it is unclosable by any string match, and PR 1.11's rule is that the
third state gets said rather than absorbed.

AND THE CRITERION IS *EXACTLY* RIGHT FOR THIS PARTICULAR ROW, not merely
adequate. The sf_events integrity argument is that there is exactly ONE stored
copy of the event-to-session link. A `count != 1` criterion is the same shape
as the property: a count of 2 is a finding because an anchor matching two sites
names one the author did not choose. An `at least once` criterion would have
been the wrong shape for this row specifically. cc's own inventory entry draws
the parallel to sabotage_control_check.py's uniqueness guard, and it holds.

ONE THING I WOULD NOT CHANGE BUT WOULD RECORD: R6's 8-character floor and
non-word-character requirement are a heuristic, and they are the only part of
the criteria that could silently drop a REAL anchor -- a genuine anchor shorter
than 8 characters, or one that is a bare identifier, is skipped rather than
checked. The tool SAYS what it skipped and why, on every run (I saw
"skipped (not an anchor, R6): '^| '" in the live output), so this is disclosed
rather than silent. That disclosure is what makes the heuristic acceptable.

=========================================================================
(2) THE A7 SPLIT -- DOES THE LIVE ARM STILL FAIL IF THE DOCUMENT STOPS BEING
    READ AT ALL?
=========================================================================

YES, ON EVERY SHAPE I COULD CONSTRUCT. TEN MUTATIONS DRIVEN, not reasoned
about: scratchpad cc_a7b_mutants_b23.py / .log. A7b's assertion is
reimplemented verbatim (exit in (CLEAN, FINDING) AND per-target anchors >= 7)
because the arm itself is hardcoded to the real repo and cannot be pointed at a
fixture. Every mutation is a tempfile tree; `git status --porcelain` on the
live clone was empty afterwards.

  M1  the document does not exist at all                   arm FAILS   exit 2, 0
